speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the
motion passes I should like to make a few remarks in reference to it. Again and again private members have protested against this way of passing divorce bills. As a member of the private bills committee I know the practice there is simply to receive the bills as they come from the Senate. The evidence is submitted to us in pamphlet form, but it is rarely read, and the bills go through the committee and the House without any consideration whatever. Occasionally bills that are controversial in character are held up, but that is very seldom. This session we have between 100 and 150 divorce bills going through all the stages of parliamentary procedure without any real consideration from this House. I understand that a bill has come to us from the Senate and has passed first reading in this House that would go a long way towards obviating the pre^nt method of conducting business-which is little less than a public scandal. The purpose of the Senate bill is to take away very largely from parliament the granting of divorces and transfer this to the courts, where it belongs. I would urgently press upon the government that, instead of setting aside the rules of 'this House, in order to get over this difficulty they should afford facilities for passing this measure, and thus put an end to this scandalous condition that for many years has prevailed.

Mr. Speaker, I would remind the Prime Minister that there are some other private bills in which some of us are interested and would like to see expedited. I have particular reference to Bill No. 177 to incorporate the Free Methodist Church in Canada. This bill has been reported from the private bills committee, but under the ordinary procedure it will not come before the House until Friday between eight and nine o'clock, and if then we should have a recurrence of what happened last night there is little hope of the bill being considered. Is there any possibility of having this bill placed in such a position that it may be disposed of by this House in the very near future, so that the Senate may have time to consider it before prorogation?

Mr. Speaker, I do not know if the hon. gentleman is aware that the bill to which he has reference was reported last night, and following the ordinary course of business it should become law before the end of the session. Everything is being done to expedite the passage of this and other bills.

I understand that
quite well. But the point I make is this: Can any special consideration be given to this bill as well as to a number of divorce bills, so that instead of having it blocked again on Friday night, thus having it held over until next week and failing to be enacted, something can be done to take care of it.

Mr. Speaker, last night a report was
brought in by general consent of the House, and there is no doubt that arrangements could be made in order to expedite bills which are not considered to be contentious. Last night business was held up, I understand, on a bill which in the opinion of some members is contentious. I have been following the business of the private bills committee carefully, and I can assure my hon. friend that I will do my very best to help along the consideration of his bill.

Mr. Speaker, will all the bills which have been reported by the committee be passed in this House if they are approved by the Senate and so become law before the session ends, or will divorce bills only get this consideration?
All bills.

maintopic: VANCOUVER HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $4,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I do not want to express
any opposition to this bill, but at this time I would like to draw the attention of the minister to certain operations of the Vancouver harbour commissioners and to suggest that the result of those operations would lead the House to believe that we should have some different system of auditing the accounts of our harbour commissioners. Of course I will have to confine myself to those matters relating to the Vancouver harbour commission. I think that a year ago the minister advised the committee of this House that there was no item in the estimates under which the operations of the Vancouver harbour board, or in fact any harbour board, could be discussed here, and that as a matter of fact the only time when we could review the expenditures of harbour commissions was when these bodies came before parliament asking for a grant of money to carry on or to extend their operations. I have here a report brought down a couple of years ago showing the earnings and expenditures of elevator No. 1, operated by the Vancouver harbour commission, for the crop year ending July 31, 1923. This return shows that the harbour commissioners received a revenue from the operations of the elevator of $203,477.96, whilst the expenditure was $106,329.10, disclosing a net operating revenue in that year of $97,148.86. Notwithstanding their large net revenue that year, the commissioners
1962	COMMONS
Vancouver Harbour Commission
advanced the handling charge from one-half cent a bushel to one cent a bushel for the following year. I have here the auditor's report of the operations of the elevator for the crop year ending July 31, 1924, which shows an operating revenue of $791,186.65, and overages for the year valued at $191,006.31. I may remark here that these overages are not shown in the balance sheet made up by the auditor but they appear under separate items. That makes total receipts of $981,192.96 for this elevator in that year, or almost a million dollars. The operating expenditure is given as $481,295.51. The total investment made by the commission in this elevator is given as $1,327,787.22, showing the operating surplus to be 36 per cent on the investment. The handling charge this year, as I said before, was one cent per bushel. There was an amount set aside for sinking fund of $71,985, leaving a net surplus of $409,310.51. Notwithstanding this very large surplus the board, in the fall of 1924, increased the harbour dues on grain from one cent to ten cents per ton. The only inference I think which can be drawn from this is that the Vancouver harbour commissioners have been using the elevator to collect from the shippers of grain a toll which is not justified by the necessities of the elevator, and, as will be shown probably later on, the harbour commissioners have used a large percentage of the revenue for capital expenditures in the harbour, amounting, I believe, to $1,800,000.
Now, I want to refer again to the auditor's statement which I have here and which I may say was procured from the department last year. On the expenditure side there is an amount of $71,284.11 for water front charge on grain handling. I hope the minister will give us an explanation of what this charge is for. There are no details given for the amount of $55,544, except to say that it is for miscellaneous expenses including administration. This seems to be rather a large amount. Then we have miscellaneous expenses, including administration and office salaries, totalling $37,674. It seems as though "administration" is included in both these items. The operating expenses are shown as $213,064, but there are no details given for this amount in the auditor's report. It appears to me, therefore, that the auditor's report cannot be considered to be complete if such a large amount is given without any details. I have been told that there were no les than three audits made of the operation of this elevator during that year, that is the crop year ending July 31, 1924, in an endeavour to show the revenue from the elevator
[Mr. Coote.l
as small as possible. Then I should like to remind the minister that in the financial statement for that year the overages, estimated at $191,006.31, were not included. The total is simply shown on the statement as "placed in reserve." Then from the operating surplus, exclusive of overages amounting to $290,000, $120,000 is shown as "transferred to reserve fund." I should also like to know now what this reserve fund amounts to. I may say that this is the only auditor's report which I have ever seen concerning the operations of the board of commissioners of the Vancouver harbour, and 1 should like, to emphasize again the necessity of having the operations of the board audited each year, and have the auditor's report available to members of parliament. This matter has been urged upon the minister upon previous occasions, but he has always refused to comply with our request that the operations of harbour commissions should be audited. But if parliament is going to make money grants to any of these boards we surely must have the privilege each year of scrutinizing their expenditures. Certainly as far as the Vancouver harbour board is concerned we are quite justified in requesting that their operations be considered by our public accounts committee.
Another item I would draw to the attention of the minister in connection with this audit is the $20,000 set aside out of the' revenue for the crop year ending July 31, 1924, to provide for overhauling and repairing the elevator for the next season's operations, although the amount of $50,000 was included in the expenditure for preparing the elevator for the season's operations in the year ending July 31, 1924. It would appear as though the commissioners were including this charge for two years instead of one. Then no explanation is given as to the waterfront charge, amounting to $71,284, except to say that it was authorized by the board at the rate of one-quarter of a cent per bushel.
The auditors also state that they have examined the various insurance policies as to amounts only and not as to wordings. Surely the auditors should have carefully examined the wording of these policies. If not, I do not see how the audit can be considered to be a complete one. The auditors also state that in the grain shipped out there were included screenings to the extent of 25,762,990 pounds, and they estimate this at 268,255 bushels. 60 pounds to the bushel, this would show a difference of 143,000 bushels.

I feel that the people of Alberta have almost as great an interest in this harbour as have the people of Vancouver. We are furnishing all the grain traffic for the port of Vancouver, and I notice that in one year, I think 1923, the quantity of grain shipped through that port was about 40 per cent of the total tonnage which was exported through it. If we had all the auditors' reports, I think we could show that more than 50 per cent of the net earnings of the port have been made from grain shipped from Alberta. I am only guessing at these figures, but at any rate a large amount of the earnings of the Vancouver harbour board have been made through the handling of Alberta grain. There has been considerable dissatisfaction in Alberta for several years over the operations of the board. More than a year ago an agitation was commenced in Alberta to have an Alberta man appointed on the Vancouver harbour board and we asked that a representative of the grain producers should be appointed to that position. There was a vacancy on the board at the time and so there was a splendid opportunity to give Alberta a representative on it. However, we were unable to persuade the government that that should be done. I do not want to blame the Minister of Marine and Fisheries for that; I do not believe he had much to say about the matter. I presume the Liberal association in Vancouver was really the body that stood in the way of such an appointment being made.
I think it was in the year 1923 that I was invited to go to Vancouver to be present at the opening of the Ballantyne pier. At that time we could not ship any grain to Vancouver from any point on the prairies because the
elevators at Vancouver were choked and the Canadian Pacific could not furnish us with cars. I went there with the intention of urging upon the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), that he should recommend to the government the granting of, say, $10,000,000 to the Vancouver harbour commission in order that more storage elevators might be erected at that point. After spending two or three days in Vancouver and looking over the operations of the then harbour board, I did not feel like taking that responsibility upon myself. I did not feel that the men who were handling that board should be entrusted with the spending of $10,000,000 in order to provide that accommodation.
I do not think we have had a satisfactory harbour commission in Vancouver since that time, and I regret that when the present board was appointed a few months ago, the government in the light of past experience did not see fit to recognize the claims of the grain producers in Alberta and to allow them to have a representative on the board. It would have been a good thing for the port of Vancouver if the Alberta grain producers had been allowed a representative on that board; it would have given the producers confidence that their interests in Vancouver were being properly looked after, and they would be much more anxious than they are at present to ship their grain through that port. Seeing that the board has been appointed I do not know that anything can be gained by urging it again upon the government at this stage; but before this bill goes through, I hope the minister will agree with us that some yearly audit should be made of the operations of this board and that these reports should be made available to parliament each year. I shall be pleased if the minister in his remarks will indicate his willingness to have this done, and as a matter of fact I would rather see him include in this bill some provision under which such an audit would be furnished to parliament each year.

The theory on which these facilities were provided is a simple one; the country guaranteed or practically put up its money to the harbour commission to enable it to provide facilities at cost-not at profit, but at cost. After providing for interest and proper allowance for depreciation and management, these facilities were to be available at cost to the people of the country, and just to the extent to which more than necessary was expended in the construction of facilities, to that extent the service rendered costs more than it should to those who use it.
I think the minister is fully aware of the intense interest which the farming population of those provinces take in these facilities. I will not enter into a discussion regarding the cost of the elevators, because that is past. But I will say this with respect to the increase that took place in the rate a year ago, that the government as such should have pressed the grain commission not to make that increase. Thereafter the rate was increased. That meant an excessive charge on the farmers for the handling of grain. It is said that the charge was not greater than that imposed at Fort William, and that is true. The early history of the Woodward elevator is as follows: A man by the name of Mr. Woodward went to Vancouver and started to build an elevator. He failed financially and the elevator was considered a white elephant on Burrard inlet. The people of Vancouver insisted that the harbour commissioners complete the elevator and put it into operation to handle grain from Alberta, because they had handled 54,000,000 bushels of grain through elevator No. 1 that year and there was a blockade; the permit system was put into effect, embargoes were placed up and down the railway line, and grain could not be moved. We needed more elevators. They made overtures to different grain companies-including the Alberta Pacific, the company of which the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) is a director, and here is what the report says:
Woodward and Company, Limited, were unable to finance to its completion the building of the elevator, and work was stopped with the completion of a working house but without the provision of any storage accommodation. Later the building was looked over by James Richardson and Sons, the United Grain Growers' Grain Company, Limited, and the Alberta Pacific Elevator Company, with a view to taking over Woodward's lease.
They turned down the proposition. Then overtures were made to other people on the prairies who might be able to handle this matter. I was asked to form a company and take it over, which I did. The commissioners were to have the plant completed for operation, grain to be handled by a lighter system in sixty days. We then bought a boat from the United States government and equipped it with the most modern machinery for transferring and handling grain, with oil burning engines and all modern equipment, at a cost of over $80,000 capable of handling 20,000 bushels per hour, with a capacity of 100,000 bushels, and that boat is still lying idle on the Pacific coast. Then I was notified two years later-after making thirty trips to Vancouver in attempts to have the plans agreed upon-that the building would be ready on June 29, and that I could take possession

Vancouver Harbour Commission
on June 30. This I could not agree to; the shipping season was over and the plant was yet unfinished. That agreement originally provided that the plant would cost $660,000 with the storage capacity, the pier, and the belt conveyors to handle grain, and we were to pay a rental of 9 per cent. I told them I could not function under those conditions, so they gave me forty-eight hours in which to accept the proposition or they would cancel the agreement, which they did. maintopic: VANCOUVER HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $4,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: The Hastings mill site was the property of the British Columbia Mills Timber & Trading Company. The harbour commission had bought these properties for the sum of $2,450,000. A cash payment of $500,000 has been made, and the balance is covered by an issue of debentures by the harbour commission, bearing interest at the rate of five per cent per annum for five years. Only a portion of that property was urgently required for developing the trackage facilities in the vicinity of the Ballantyne pier. When the pier was built the erection of an elevator was not contemplated. Owing to the construction of the elevator the trackage facilities of the pier were interfered with. It was considered necessary to extend the trackage facilities and it was proposed to expropriate part of the Hastings mill property for that purpose. But, instead of expropriating a part of that property, it was considered advisable to buy the whole property and the harbour commission have taken for their own use the part of the property that was to be expropriated. The remaining portion has been leased to the British Columbia Mills Timber & Trading Company for a period of five years. The rental paid by this company for the balance of this property is sufficient to take care of the interest on the bonds issued by the harbour commission. Disbursements have been made to the extent of $500,000 and the balance is covered by an issue of debentures which are being taken care of by the rent received from that company. It is well known to everyone familiar with the conditions that this property, by reason of its central location, is one of the most valuable in the harbour. It will be required in the very near future, and the companies which are somewhat interested in the development of the harbour at Vancouver, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National railways both suggested to the harbour commission that they should acquire that property. The amount has been fixed by arbitration.

Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved,-That it is expedient to bring in
a measure,-
1.	To provide for a Federal District Commission and to repeal the acts respecting the Ottawa Improvement Commission;
2.	To authorize the payment to the commission of the sum of $250,000 a year for a period not exceeding sixteen years from the first day of April, 1927, and to make provision for borrowing powers, the issue of debentures and the repayment thereof.
Federal District Commission
Explain.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My purpose
at the moment is simply to have the bill introduced so that hon. members may read its provisions before time is taken up with detailed discussion. The purpose of the bill to be founded on the resolution is to extend somewhat the powers of the present Ottawa Improvement Commission by enlarging the area over which it will be authorized to carry on its work, increasing the amount of money at its disposal, and changing its name to conform more accurately with the intent and purpose of the commission. The Ottawa Improvement Commission was established in the year 1899 in order to undertake the beautification of the capital of Canada. From time to time its membership has been increased, as has been also the sum placed at its disposal. This increase has been made for the reason, that with the development of the work of the commission there goes inevitably an extra obligation of maintenance, and I am advised that at the present time the amount voted by parliament to the commission is used very largely for the maintenance of the parks and drivewaj's which have already been constructed.
The country is fortunate in having at the moment at the head of the commission an exceptionally able business executive in the person of Mr. Thomas Ahearn, and the commission have been laying their plans for the further improvement of the capital. They believe they can make better headway with their work il an opportunity is given them to plan operations over a number of years, and for that reason the bill proposes to confer upon the commission that additional power. The amount at present at the disposal of the commission is $150,000 per annum. It is proposed in this bill to increase that sum by $100,000. It is not so much the city of Ottawa as it is the capital of Canada that is being considered. It is a national obligation to make the capital of our Dominion as attractive as possible, and, as hon. members know, for years past the government has felt in that regard, a special responsibility. The use of the term " Ottawa " as applied to the commission is somewhat misleading inasmuch as the environs, the immediate surroundings, are quite as important, from the standpoint of beautification of the capital, as is the city proper. Indeed, it is with the outlying parts of the city including the opposite side of the river that much of the work of improvement will be carried on.
I might add this further feature, as pointed out to me by the chairman of the commission.

Federal District Commission
The capital has grown materially since some of the existing improvements were effected, and many of the driveways are to-day much too small in view of the increased motor traffic. As a matter of fact they are too small to be safe, and they will have to be considerably enlarged. This work cannot be undertaken by the commission until some additional appropriation is made for the purpose. The other features deserving of consideration will,
I think, be apparent once the bill is introduced.
How much, roughly speaking, has been expended by the government of Canada in the past in this connection? How much have we contributed toward the beautification of Ottawa?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have not the details with me but I will endeavour to have a statement prepared and will give my hon. friend the figures when the bill is being discussed.

speakeroldname: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
For myself, I am heartily in
accord with the proposal contained in the resolution. I have watched the development that has taken place in the city of Ottawa for over a quarter of a century, and my great regret is that the improvement has gone on so slowly. I had the privilege some days ago, of discussing this matter for a few minutes with the chairman of the Ottawa Improvement Commission, and I told him that in my view his request was entirely inadequate for the purpose. I believe the sum now suggested is too small. We should start on a larger scale extended over a longer term of years, and should let it be definitely understood that a certain substantial sum annually shall be set aside to make the capital of the country what it should be and what nature intended it to be. I doubt whether there is a capital in the world so splendidly endowed by nature as is the capital of Canada; and by capital I do not mean the immediate surroundings, but the adjacent country as well. I believe we shall be doing something of which we ourselves shall be proud, and which people of the country will approve, if we adopt even a more extended scale than that submitted by the government. If $150,000 is required for the annual upkeep, the extra $100 000 will not do a great deal in the sixteen years which is fixed in the resolution as the time limit. I hope to live to see this capital something like the capital visualized by Sir Wilfrid Laurier over twenty-seven years ago when he said that he would like to see Ottawa made the Washington of the North. Washington entered upon a scheme involving a 
twenty-five year program with a financial obligation amounting to about $20,000,000 per annum. We of course will not attempt anything like that, but it seems to me that now we are dealing with the matter we might extend the proposal somewhat.

As
I live in the city of Ottawa and always have done so, although I represent a constituency in Quebec, I want to say a few words just to show that I am in accord with the suggestion put forward by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and with the appropriate words which have come from the leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie). All of us are, I think, agreed that the natural surroundings of Ottawa are as beautiful as those of any city in the world. I have travelled a good deal and I have yet to see a more beautiful city.
What about Halifax?

Halifax too is
beautiful, but I would not put it above Ottawa. And that is high praise indeed. In my opinion, with one exception, Ottawa is as fine a place to live in as any I know of in the world. I will not enter into all the details now, but there is one regard in which this city can be improved, apart from any question of beautification. We have drinking water secured from the Ottawa river and made potable by artificial means, but it seems to me that with so many lakes close by we surely ought to have in this city a natural supply of water obtained from the beautiful lakes north in the Gatineau country. Most of the people in Ottawa who can afford to do so buy Tally-Ho or other waters instead of drinking the Ottawa water, and that is hardly fair to the poor, who should have a constant supply of pure water. I know of nothing more conducive to the health of the citizens than an abundant supply of absolutely pure water. I do not. desire to criticize this resolution or to suggest any changes, but I do say to the Prime Minister that in the very influential position which he occupies and from the fact that he is now bringing in a resolution to provide more money to be used by this commission in doing this service to the city and to the government, he might impress upon the authorities of the city of Ottawa that as the government is assisting in this way and is prepared to go perhaps further in years to come, it is the duty of the city to see that a proper water supply is secured from the northern hills.

Federal District Commission

The unanimity of opinion
expressed so far from both sides of the House makes me somewhat doubtful as to the wisdom of accepting this proposition without some criticism, because it is always an unhealthy sign to me when I see both sides of the House in such complete agreement as they appear to be with regard to this resolution. The city of Ottawa is the capital city of Canada, and I agree with all that has been said with regard to its beautiful situation, its natural attractions and so on. But, though I may be the only one in the House who takes this, position, I am not altogether prepared to give my assent to the spending of millions of dollars in beautifying this city of Ottawa while there are public works in various parts of the country which are absolutely neglected, and to which no consideration whatever is given. If in connection with the proposition to make this city the Washington of the North in a country of 9,000,000 people as compared with a country of 120,000.000 people it is proposed to carry out those ideas by tearing down such a building as the post office, for instance, which I think is a part of the plan, while people in my constituency must receive their mail in a place not much better than a box car or a packing case, and while I can get no consideration from the government in that regard, then I say that for one I am not prepared to give my whole-hearted support to a proposition of this kind even though it meets with the approval of most of the members on both sides of this House.
We are placed alongside the United States, which is a very large country with a great population and great wealth; we are a small country so far as population is concerned, and I do not think we should forget the fact that we have passed through a war which has left a heavy burden of debt on this Dominion. I know that when members of this House apply, as they have the right to apply in the interests of those parts of the country which they represent, for much needed public works, they are met each time with the figures of the national debt we are carrying and the responsibilities which we have to meet in that connection, But when it comes to providing wider streets for the larger population of Ottawa, to improving the water supply or doing things of that nature to the interest and benefit of those who live in Ottawa, I say it is up to the members of this House to take into consideration other parts of the country which are being forced to wait for matters which are more justly entitled to consideration
than the tearing down of splendid buildings here in Ottawa, which are now serving their purposes and would continue to serve their purposes admirably for many years to come.
Before this bill goes through I will have an opportunity of discussing it, in common with other members, more fully. I do not wish to be understood as opposing a reasonable expenditure in connection with the beautifying of this city; we have certain responsibilities in that regard, but I do say that we should not feel it incumbent upon us to keep in mind these particular responsibilities and utterly ignore those other matters which have been long waiting for consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I have been waiting for the two Ottawa members to speak on this resolution; they have not done so, but since some 15,000 people in the west end of the city are included in my riding, perhaps I might be permitted to say a few words.
In the first place I must disagree with the hon. member for Frontenae-Addington (Mr. Edwards). We must not forget that while this amount of money is spent in beautifying this city, in return the city gives free fire protection, exemption from taxes and so on. I quite believe that to-day the city would be further ahead if it collected these taxes from the government, as it would from any private individual, .and paid for its own improvements. I desire to support this resolution to the utmost of my ability, and I agree with the leader of the opposition when he says that the amount should not be $250,000 but $500,000. To increase the amount by only $100,000 is a mere bagatelle. The driveways in the west end and the bridges which will be constructed to the province of Quebec will take up a great deal of that money, and very little will be left for other things during the next few years. The amount is not nearly what it should be, and I would be very glad if the Prime Minister could see bis way clear to double it.

I would like to ask whether before this bill passes we will have a comprehensive idea as to the way in which this money is to be spent. Have the commissioners any plan in mind, or are we just voting the money to the commission to be expended as they may see fit in the beautification of this city? I am rather inclined to agree in many respects with the hon. member for Frontenae-Addington (Mr. Edwards). We do not begrudge the city of Ottawa anything; we would like to see Ottawa made a worthy capital of this Dominion, but
197S

Federal District Commission
there is a limit to the distance we may go and to the amount of money we may vote without knowing how it is going to be expended. I happen to know that the matter of a pure water supply would be very expensive, but is no doubt very justifiable, and some of this money might well be expended in purifying the air of this 'city as well. One has only to walk down the streets of this city to come to the conclusion that the first thing we should get away from is the smell of brimstone which is always in the air.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

Might I ask the Prime Minister why it is proposed to give the commission power to issue bonds? I do not suppose that they will be constructing anything which will bring in revenue, so it would seem to me that the money should be provided directly by parliament each year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There are certain works of construction to be carried' on, the commission can plan ahead for a few years, ic they have power to issue debentures. The bill provides that any obligations arising out of the issue of securities become a first charge on the moneys appropriated. This simply enables the commission to plan ahead with a greater degree of certainty than if they were dependent upon annual appropriations. The total appropriation by parliament will not as a consequence 'be increased.

If the bill simply provides
for an annual grant of so much to the commission-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is all.

-I was wondering why this
procedure was adopted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It simply allows the commission to use a part of the grant as the years go by toward meeting payments due on securities they may issue. They will not issue securities unless they igain some substantial advantage by so doing.

I understood the Prime Minister to say that it was the intention to enlarge the area over which the commission would have control. How large an area is the commission to be given control of under this proposal?
Peace River.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think the commission will attempt to deal with Peace River. The purpose is not to confine the work of the commission to the city of

Ottawa but to include -the suburbs of the city and the city of Hull across the way. Before the commission can extend the area, they will have to submit their proposals to the governor in council and those proposals will have to be approved. I assume that the commission has no thought of going beyond the immediate suburbs of the city. I have seen some mention in the press that this bill would include provision for a national park. That is an idea entirely separate; it has nothing to do with the present measure at all. I want to make that clear. I should like to say, however, that I do think a national park in the vicinity of Ottawa is something that is very much in the public interest, and that provision should be made for it at once, but that has nothing to do with this particular measure.

I do not want to oppose this resolution in any way. I should like to say, however, that every time I walk down from the parliament buildings I cannot help but feel that Canada has not been very well served by her politicians in years past so far as beautifying the national capital is concerned. There is not a street in Ottawa from which the main entrance to the parliament buildings can be seen until you reach Wellington street.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.

It seems to me that our
legislators and our governments for the past twenty years have been very remiss in their duties in that they did not, before Sparks street was built up with such expensive buildings, expropriate the property for about three blocks between Wellington street and Sparks street, and open a wide thoroughfare immediately opposite the main entrance to the parliament buildings. The rest of that property could have been used for government buildings in which to house the different public departments-buildings of a character which would beautify the capital and would be in harmony with the architectural design of the parliament buildings themselves. I do not know whether it is too late to do anything of that nature. I suppose those who come twenty years after will say that we might have done it. Possibly the state of the public finances to-day would not permit the necessary expenditure, but I think it is something that the commission might very well consider. The commission have done a lot to beautify the city of Ottawa, but I sometimes think they have not taken advantage of the improvements they have made in the

Federal District Commission
capital. They have constructed miles of beautiful driveways, but they have never secured control of the property along those driveways. Once a driveway is completed the property adjacent to it becomes very valuable residential property, and the value which is created by the construction of the driveway has gone to benefit private individuals. Most of the people who bought that property and constructed homes are benefiting from the unearned increment accruing from the increase in the value of the land. I think if the improvement commission are going to construct other driveways they should secure control of the property along those driveways. If that is done they will secure some revenue from the increase in the value of the property. I do not want to indulge in any destructive remarks with respect to this proposal. I would prefer to make suggestions of a constructive nature. I hope the commission, with the approval of the government, will go so far at least as to secure control of the property along any new driveway they may construct, and thus secure some revenue from these improvements.

I would ask if a comprehensive scheme has been adopted by the commission looking to the future, when this city will have a population of 500,000 or more? Failure to do that on the part of large cities to-day, both in Canada and the United States, has resulted in the loss of hundreds of thousands of dollars, yes millions, to the municipalities concerned. No doubt the eminent business men on the commission have looked into this matter, but it is just as well to point out the situation to them, and sound a note of warning as to what is likely to happen if a comprehensive scheme is not adopted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The commission have taken the very course which my hon. friend has indicated should be taken. I have in my hand, submitted to me by the chairman of the commission, some of the plans the commission wish to be free to carry out. I do not think it would be in the public interest to disclose these proposals at present, but they do reveal exactly what my hon. friend has in mind, namely, foresight on the part of the commission in laying out constructive plans for future developments.

May I ask the Prime Minister if he considers it proper to give us an idea of how far afield that foresight goes? He intimated it might carry us to Hull. There is the town of Aylmer, Quebec, where I think some improvements might be made. There is also the town of Cornwall, and other places within a hundred miles of Ottawa. I wonder how far the environs spoken of aTe supposed to extend? Perhaps they will take in Sydenham, where I hope the Minister of Finance will see his way clear to provide a decent post office, when he is providing money for this scheme to beautify the city of Ottawa.

Will the Prime Minister be good enough to tell us what the capital expenditure will be in connection with this proposal? I have a good deal of sympathy with the desire to beautify the city of Ottawa, but it would be a good thing if my right hon. friend would visit some of the back communities in this country who have been trying to get rural mail delivery, or some improvement in their postal facilities, in order to keep people on the land, something they are trying to do in every province in Canada. I tell my right hon. friend that these people deserve sympathy and consideration from the public treasury first, before the city of Ottawa. I think we ought to do something for them. If we are going into a huge capital expenditure, and this grant is to be mortgaged for the future to pay interest for twenty-five or thirty years, I think we ought to go pretty slowly, or know at all events what we are going to do.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall the resolution
carry?
No; I think we ought to know what the capital expenditure will be.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I may say
that the commission is expected to keep within the amount that is appropriated by parliament. Before bringing the proposal to the House, I asked for a statement as to how it was proposed the moneys would be used, and the proposals of the commission relate and are confined to the grant which parliament is putting at their disposal.
What are the proposals with respeot to capital expenditure and how much are they going to mortgage the future of the country for?

The bill provides for
14,000,000 and it states that this $4,000,000 will be paid within a. period of sixteen years at the rate of $250,000 a year. The advantage of this is that the commission know beforehand exactly how much they will receive and thus they can finance more easily. Last week I had the pleasure of meeting Sir George

Federal District Commission
Garneau who is at the head of the Battlefields Memorials Commission. He was suggesting that we should adopt for his commission the same system and that, instead of voting yearly the sum of $100,000, we should once for all make it statutory so that the banks and other financial institutions might know exactly how much the commission received and how much they could expect to get. This bill will cover that in this case.

I do not think the government is going far enough. What should be done now is to declare Ottawa and such part of its suburbs as might be thought desirable, a federal district, to appoint a commission to govern the city of Ottawa, and to treat the people of the city as the people of Washington are treated. If we are going to make the city of Ottawa a great capital, attractive in all its physical features, the way to go about the matter is to appoint a commission now to take over the city. Lest this government manage and govern it. We have a splendid precedent for that across the border and that precedent could be followed with great advantage to the country.
What is proposed, as I understand this legislation, is to make a grant of $4,000,000 covering sixteen years. That looks to me as though the creation of a federal district in Ottawa will be postponed for at least sixteen years. If there were as much foresight in the government as there seems to be in the commission that is about to be appointed, what I am proposing should be done. Instead of appointing a new commission now and making new conditions for the commission to act upon, we should at this time decide the question: Shall Ottawa foe a federal district? If the answer is in the affirmative, then we should proceed to appoint a commission, take over the government -of the city and direct its affairs in the same way as is done in Washington.

I
entirely differ, Sir, from the opinion of the hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken) who suggests creating a federal district. On the other hand, it is with pleasure that I support the resolution of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) by which it is proposed to spend in Ottawa, Hull and their surroundings a sum of $4,000,000 in the course of the next sixteen years.	, ]

On behalf of my constituents I am absolutely opposed to the city of Hull becoming part of a federal district, because it would despoil us of our most cherished rights. We are perfectly content with our fate and we wish to remain a part of the province of Quebec. The resolution introduced by the right hon. Prime Minister to establish a commission having very extensive authority and empowered to spend money over the whole district, is approved by all, but I do not think it in any way necessary to create a federal district which would include Hull, this would, I again state, deprive us of the rights which we have enjoyed ever since confederation.

speakeroldname: Hon. LUCIEN CANNON (Acting Minister of Justice):
speechtext:
As I explained when the resolution was before the House, the object of the bill is to provide for the appointment of a successor to Colonel Biggar, who at present is the Chief Electoral Officer. Colonel Biggar has intimated his wish to relinquish the office. Section 1 provides that the Chief Electoral Officer in future shall be appointed by a resolution of the House of Commons and that his salary will be $6,000 a year. When discussing the resolution the hon. member for St. Lawrenee-lSt. George (Mr. Cahan) raised the question as to tenure of office of the Chief Electoral Officer, and upon examining the bill as it is drafted I discovered that provision has not been made for that. I have placed an amendment in the hands of the Chairman. I move to add the words "per annum" to the second paragraph of section 1, so that it will read:
The Chief Electoral Officer shall be appointed by resolution of the House of Commons and shall be paid a salary of $6,000 per annum.
That is the section as it stands in the bill, plus the words "per annum." I also propose to add the words:
He shall hold office on the same tenure and shall he removable only for cause and in the same manner as a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada.
Adding these words removes any possibility of the post of Chief Electoral Officer becoming somewhat of a political position and the holder being removed by resolution of the House, without any of the guarantees that should surround such an office.

Will the
minister tell me:	When the chief electoral
officer w'as appointed, at what salary, and if he vacates the office will he receive a pension, and if so how much?

Colonel Biggar was the
first Chief Electoral Officer under the new electoral law passed in 1920. I will give the House the reason for the amending act. By
consulting the Dominion Elections Act hon. members will see that the name of Colonel Biggar was inserted in the clause when the bill was originally passed, so that Colonel Biggar was appointed in 1920. The salary which he is receiving is $12,000 a year. He was performing, in addition to the functions of Chief Electoral Officer, the duties of counsel for the government. When he retires Colonel Biggar will be entitled, in common with every officer or official who retires, to a certain leave of absence. We provide in this bill that the vacancy Shall occur on June 30. He will receive no pension after his retirement.

I am very
glad to hear that, not that I have anything against the Chief Electoral Officer, but I think that principle might have been adopted more generally than it has been in times past. I have sometimes been led to think that we have almost as many pensioned civil servants as we have active civil servants in the country. In spite of the fact that I -may arouse the indignation of some members of the legal profession, I say that I have felt, whether rightly or wrongly, that they have certainly looked after men of the legal profession when it came to the fixing of salaries for judges and looking after the retirement of these judges. They leave the bench very often, because, as they tell us their health would not stand the strain of the work on the bench, and they have actually left the bench with good big pensions. I might name the former Minister of Justice the Hon. C. J. Doherty, who left the bench under these conditions.
Hear, hear.

My hon,
friend would not be so ready with his " hear, hear ", if I named someone on his own side. But these men have left the bench because they could not stand the strain of the hard work on the bench, and have gone into the very mild occupation of politics-off the bench into politics. When they could not stand the strain of politics they retired and again took judgeships, and if they continue that procedure in time they will be drawing three or four pensions, if they live long enough. As soon as the provinces pass the necessary legislation with reference to old age pensions they will also come in under that act and will be drawing a little more. I say that we have gone to a ridiculous extreme in providing salaries, specially for men on the bench, and providing big superannuation when they retire, probabl.v, in just as good health as any of us in this chamber to-day, I say

that it would be a good general principle to adopt if we paid a man on the bench whatever he was worth as is done in other occupations, and let him provide for his old age out of the salary he got, just as other people do. It is ridiculous to give a man ten or twelve thousand dollars a year and then make provision for his old age. If he has not sense enough to provide for his old age out of ten thousand a year he has not sense enough to be on the bench. This system of superannuation of officers and judges has been carried on in this country, all because we have a lot of men in this House who are of the legal profession, and are looking ahead to the day when they will step out of politics, drop into a fat job on the bench and then retire on a pension which will keep them for the rest of their days. This thing has been carried to a ridiculous extreme. We have carried this system to the matter of appointments to commissions. Is there a man or woman in Canada, outside of the immediate people concerned, who believes that Newton Wesley Rowell is worth a fee of $290 a day, $20 a day for living allowance and his travelling expenses, while working on that commission? He could not earn that money if he were not working on a commission. Millions of dollars are being spent in that way.
I do not propose to let this matter drop, I will bring it up on future occasions, so that the government will not forget it. I will protest against these expenditures, just as long as there are public works throughout the country which are thrown to one side, absolutely disregarded and nothing done to meet the public needs in that respect, when we have millions to spend for the purpose of beautifying Ottawa and millions to spend providing judges with good fat jobs, millions to spend on them when they get too old or too lazy to sit on the bench, and large amounts to spend on political pets who are appointed to this or that commission, because these men have not provided themselves with a sufficient sum to enable them to retire when they get a little older. That is the slate of affairs in this country and it is a crime.

speechtext: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved that the House go into committee of supply.

maintopic: NATURALIZATION OF CANADIAN WOMEN MARRIED TO ALIENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are many Canadian women who resent the injustice which women who are British subjects, but married to aliens, suffer in regard to naturalization. A woman may be a Canadian, she may be the grandchild of Canadians, but if she marries an alien she ceases to be a British subject. She may not resume her British nationality until her husband chooses to become naturalized; and if he dies or the marriage is dissolved the woman remains an alien until she makes a declaration and obtains a certificate from the Secretary of State. It would seem that such treatment makes naturalization of small account. It must be of little importance if adults can be naturalized without satisfying the condition as to desirability and without being required to take the oath of allegiance, and it certainly is insulting to women to assume that their allegiance can be transferred without their own consent.
Under the present law marriage and citizenship are very much mixed up. I don't think the two should be so closely related, if related at all. There are scores of British women resident in Canada who, having married aliens, find themselves citizens of no country, unable to claim the protection of any government, unable to vote, unable to teach or to accept any civil position should the need arise, and, in the event of their husbands' death, unable to participate in the mother's allowance for
the benefit of their children. Because of their statelessness they find it almost impossible to obtain a passport. I have * a letter from a woman in Ontario received when the resolution in regard to this subject appeared on the order paper. She lives in Prince Edward county and pays taxes, but at the last election on December 1 not only herself but twenty-five other women in the county were prevented from voting. She tells that her great grandfather was an officer in the Revolutionary war and a British subject and she describes how loyal they had always been; yet after marriage to an American, although they live in Canada and she owns large property and pays taxes, she finds herself unable 'to vote in any election in this country. She writes protesting against such treatment.
Last year I tried to get a passport for an *Ontario girl who was married to an alien. I could not obtain the passport and she had to *cancel her trip. Many other members of this House could tell similar stories. I have heard them in private conversation and if they had the opportunity to speak I am sure they could tell of experiences such as I have described. When it is considered that, in western Canada particularly, we are receiving from many shores aliens who are marrying women of British nationality, this is a matter of vital concern to Canada.
The right of women to retain their British nationality although married to aliens was enjoyed until the year 1870. Previous to that time the common law of England contained two principles: first, that a British woman who married an alien should retain her British nationality, and, secondly, that an alien woman who married a British subject remained an alien. Women were regarded as chattels; *after marriage they had no right to their property, which passed into the control of their husbands. They did not possess the franchise and generally they were in a humiliating and subordinate position as compared to the status of women to-day. Yet until 1870 they had the right to retain their nationality. In that year the law was changed to provide that a married woman should be deemed to be the subject of the state of which her husband for the [DOT]time being was a subject. When this change was made the women of Great Britain-for this is British law-were not consulted at all, and the subject received very little debate in [DOT]the House of Commons, through which it passed very hurriedly. The law was amended in 1914 to read:
That the wife of a British subject shall be deemed to be a British subject and the wife of an alien shall be deemed to be an alien.
Naturalization oj Women

In the amending act of 1914, however, women did make certain gains. In the British nationality and Status of Aliens Act, 1914, women gained the principle, excluded since 1870, that a woman might be of different nationality from her husband's. If her British husband should change his nationality, she might under the act declare that she would remain British; and a British-born woman with a foreign husband may now apply, on the dissolution of her marriage by death or divorce, for readmission to British nationality without complying with the requirements as to residence.
In 1922 Lord Danesfort brought forward a bill, which passed its second reading, contain-' ing two "important principles: first, British women should have the right to retain their nationality when they married aliens; and, second, that an alien woman should not by the mere act of marriage with a British subject become a British subject. Dissolution of parliament prevented anything further being done, but in 1923 a' select committee of the Lords and Commons was appointed to consider the subject. This committee, comprising five commoners and five lords, agreed that a change was necessary. But, one of the lords dissenting, no recommendations were made when the report was presented. The objection advanced by this dissenting lord was that the change would result in trouble in the home. Men and women, it was urged, were one. We all know that, but the thing I want to know is, which one? If it is going to disturb the harmony of the home to have any change of nationality on the part of either husband or wife, let the husband take the nationality of the wife. It is as fair that way as the other.
I have no great fear that the home will be disrupted if women are given the vote, or if they go to work, or if they retain their nationality. Every advance made by woman has been frowned upon because of this very fear of the home being disrupted. Men are always worried about this consequence, but it does not happen, for the simple reason that the real home is a community of interests so strong that it will take more than any change of nationality, more than the vote or any of these things to disrupt it. We need not worry about the home on that account.
The matter was brought forward again in the British House of Commons in 1925, when Major Harvey introduced a resolution, which was carried, to the following effect:
'that in the opinion of this House a British woman should not lose or be deemed to lose her nationality by mere act of marriage with an alien, but that it should be open to her to make declaration of alienage.
[Miss Macphail.l
During the course of the debate on that resolution the Under Secretary of State informed the House that after the meeting of the joint committee of the Lords and Commons to which I have referred, no agreement having been reached, the matter had been raised at the imperial conference of 1923. It was referred to a sub-committee of the conference, as will be found at page 1213 of that conference. The suggestions of the sub-committee of the conference as well as those of the joint committee of the Lords and Commons were submitted to the dominions in the autumn of 1924, but up to the time when Major Harvey was taking part in the debate on the resolution I have quoted, only one of the dominions had expressed itself on the subject. I wonder why Canada did not reply. I believe that public opinion in this country favours a change. I have no doubt it is the desire of the people of this Dominion that a British woman married to an alien shall have the right to retain her British nationality. Mr. Hurst, speaking to Major Harvey's resolution in 1925, said:
I do not believe we ought to wait until the principle adopted in this resolution has been accepted by all self-governing dominions. On July 14, 1921, I put a question to the then Prime Minister on this subject and I was told that no decision could be arrived at until the dominions had been consulted with. That is four years ago and we are not one inch further along the road to legislation than we were then.
From the beginning we can conclude that the British House of Commons on various occasions has wanted to do something about the matter. As I have pointed out, they referred the question of the dominions, from only one of which they received any reply. I cannot see why they did not hear from our Dominion, and I think it is time the parliament of this country took whatever steps are' necessary to make it possible for British women married to aliens to retain their own nationality.
The United States tried the law which we now have for the period from 1907 to 1922 when, by the Cable act, the law was changed to read:
A woman citizen of the United States shall not cease to be a citizen by reason of her marriage unless she makes a formal renunciation of her citizenship before a court having jurisdiction over naturalization of aliens.
It was further enacted that:
Any woman who marries a citizen of the United States shall not become a citizen by reason of such marriage.
By this law an American girl who marries a Canadian becomes a British subject while still remaining a citizen of the United States, but a Canadian girl who marries an American

Naturalization of Women
ceases to be a British subject and does not become a citizen of the United States, and is therefore a citizen of no country. There are many practical examples of this, and I am sure every member of this House is aware of some of them. The republics of Argentine, Brazil and Chile have similar naturalization laws to those of the United States. Belgium in 1922 gave women the right to retain their nationality after marriage if they so desired. In 1924 Sweden gave women the same right, so long as they remained in Sweden, and other Scandinavian countries have followed the same procedure.
Resolutions asking for this change have been passed by women's organizations in Canada for many years past, among those outstanding being the National Council of Women, who have time and again asked that women be naturalized of their own right, and that marriage to an alien should not affect them in any way. The Canadian Council of Agriculture have presented this question to the cabinet almost times without number. The Womens' Institutes of Canada have taken a firm stand upon it, together with the Social Service Council of Canada. The Alberta legislature on two occasions adopted resolutions dealing 'with this problem, one of which was introduced last session by Hon. Irene Parlby and seconded by Mrs. Nellie McClung, but no action was taken in this House. As
on looking at the order paper I found the resolution touching this subject appearing under the name of the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail). Upon inquiry of the Clerk of the House I found that the hon. member called yesterday at the office of the Clerk and asked that the notice be dropped, in order to enable her to bring up the matter. The order was given, but the printer neglected to make the change.

Might we not expect a statement from the Prime Minister in connection with this matter?
I have already pointed out, Great Britain adopted Major Harvey's resolution in 1924, and I do not see why the parliament of Canada has not taken some stand on this question.
I realize that this is an international matter, but after all it will not be dealt with in an international way until all the countries affected deal with it first, and I appeal to the members of this House in the name of the womanhood of this country to see that this injustice is removed and that women have the same right of citizenship accorded to men. I think women love their country as much as men, and since women are not to-day property as they were thought to be in days gone by, but thinking individuals, I appeal to this House of Commons to take the first opportunity to do all that can be done in this matter. Let it be taken up by the League of Nations or the next Imperial conference; let us do anything that can be done in order to remove this injustice.

the House to the fact that the discussion was not in order so long as the motion of the hon. member still appeared on the order paper. Having given some study to this very interesting question I am only too sorry that the hon. member did not have an opportunity to bring it before the House in another way, but I quite realize that private members days were practically blocked by one private bill during much of the time of *the session, and that was the main reason why this particular motion was never reached. The House will also understand that at this stage of the session, and considering also the way in which this motion has been taken up, it is not my intention to go fully into the question, but rather to state very briefly the policy of the government in this regard.
I wish to make a distinction between the principle involved in the question brought forward by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) and the practicability of making any amendment to the Naturalization Act at the present time. As to the principle entailed in this question, I am quite willing to state that the government is fully in accord with the attitude of the hon. member. We believe that it would be desirable that women of British nationality should be entitled to retain British nationality aftei marriage to an alien, if they so desire. At the same time the House will appreciate the fact that the Naturalization Act in Canada is based upon the imperial act and' that it would not be wise to amend it in any way of our own accord, without taking into consideration the effects of such an amendment within the empire. The existing act in Canada is the result of what may be called a contract entered into between Great Britain and the dominions at the Imperial conference of 1911. I will not give the full agreement, but will mention only the most important points, one being that imperial nationality should be world-wide and uniform, and the other that the imperial act should be so framed as to enable the self-governing dominions to adopt it. Inasmuch as the act in Canada is based upon the imperial act it may be interesting to note the evolution of the latter statute. My hon. friend (Miss Macphail), in the course of her very interesting remarks, has referred to some phases of that evolution. It is noteworthy that in early days the situation in England approached more closely to what my hon. friend now desires than what it does to-day. By the common law of England, prior to 1844, the nationality of a woman was not affected by her manage. If a British woman subject married an alien, she remained British.
[Mr. Kinfret.)
If an alien woman married a British subject, she remained an alien. It was not until 1844 and 1870 that the act in Great Britain was amended. The amendment brought forward in 1S44 was to the effect "that any woman married or who shall be married to a natural-bom subject or person naturalized shall be deemed and taken to be herself naturalized and have all the rights and privileges of a natural-bom subject." This did alter one phase of the situation in this respect, that an alien woman marrying a British subject by that fact became herself a British subject. In 1870 the other side of the question was taken up and this amendment was enacted in Great Britain that a "married woman shall be deemed to be a subject of the state of which her husband is for the time being a subject". That is to say, by these two amendments in 1844 and 1870 the British parliament had departed altogether from the original common law. In 1914, as my hon. friend has pointed out, the law was reenacted in simpler and dearer form, and it was stated that "the wife of a British subject shall be deemed a British subject, and the wife of an alien be deemed to be an alien". But from that date until now the whole trend of opinion in the British parliament has been to depart from the act of 1914 by making a number of exceptions to this ironclad rule.
I do not think I should go into the matter very fully to-day except to state that in 1923 a select committee in England took evidence on the matter. They were not unanimous in their report, but the majority of the committee were in favour of amending the law according to the principle invoked by my hon. friend to-day, and according to the motion that she placed on the order paper. In 1925 Major Harvey moved a resolution in the British House of Commons to the effect that a British woman should not lose or be deemed to lose her nationality by the mere act of marriage with an alien, but it was to be open to her to make a declaration of allegiance. That resolution was adopted. In the following year, in 1926, a similar motion was moved and adopted by the Australian parliament. Therefore it will be seen that the trend of opinion in the empire is against the iron-clad provision that was enacted in the British parliament in 1914, due no doubt to the situation created by the war at that time. I would, however, point out that in both the British parliament and the commonwealth of Australia it was made very clear that the whole question should not be decided separately by either parliament, but that it

Naturalization of Women
should be decided unanimously by all the .parliaments within the empire, it being desirable that unanimity should be observed in the framing of naturalization acts throughout the empire. The reason for that is very plain. We could, even within the agreement of 1911 to which I alluded at the beginning of my remarks, frame our act separately and according to our own views, but the effect would be to grant naturalization only within our own borders, and would create a confusing situation which I think my hon. friend himself will admit is not at all desirable. It is for that reason that the whole question was submitted to the Imperial conference in 1926 with the hope of arriving at a common solution. I regret to say that the hope was not realized, although I am informed that during the discussion the Canadian repesentatives not only took a stand favourable to the principle we are discussing to-day but they advanced the situation somewhat towards a solution. I refer my hon. friend to the report of the Imperial conference of 1926, page 32, which contains the conclusion of the conference on that matter:
The committee also considered the question of the nationality of married women. On this matter some divergence of view was disclosed and the committee were unable to arrive at a unanimous conclusion. Since, however, they attached great importance to the maintenance of uniformity throughout the various parts of the empire in the law relating to British nationality, they decided to recommend to the conference that further consideration of the question should be postponed pending the report of the committee of experts referred to in the report of the Inter-imperial Relations Committee which, it is proposed, should deal with various matters connected with the operation of Dominion legislation, and in view of the possibility of an attempt being made to regulate the problem of dual nationality and no nationality by international agreement. The conference adopted this recommendation.
That is wheTe the matter stands, and I think I might well conclude my remarks now, by stating that the government is fully in accord with the hon. member for Southeast Grey as to the principle of her motion, but we believe that no attempt to amend the Naturalization Act should be made now. It would be better merely to proclaim that principle, and make it known to the imperial authorities and to other parliaments within the empire that on this matter Canada stands with the British and Australian parliaments. But we desire uniformity in the matter of this law, and we think that no specific amendment should be considered at present.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
maintopic: NATURALIZATION OF CANADIAN WOMEN MARRIED TO ALIENS
speechtext:
May I say just a few words
in support of the proposal of the hon. member for Southeast Grey. I quite realize that there are many complicated questions arising with respect to naturalization. No question is in fact more difficult. But may I suggest that if we insist that we can do nothing in Canada until there be uniform action all over the British Empire it may mean that a very great hardship may be worked on a great many of our own Canadian citizens. The hon. membeT for Southeast Grey called attention to the situation in which some of our own people find themselves. I have had letters on the subject. I think of one in particular from a woman in British Columbia who was married to an American. Her husband deserted her and she was left in a most awkward position. She has no standing as an American citizen under the American law. Under the Canadian law she is not a British subject although she is Britiish-born. Short of the death of her husband, which apparently is not likely to take place for some time, there seems to be no way by which she can regain her Canadian citizenship. One case of that kind <is sufficient to point out the need of some action on our part. I can understand that in Great Britain where social distinctions between England and Europe are considerable, they may not have such practical difficulties as we have in Canada. But in this country, when we have 3,000 miles of an international boundary with two peoples of the same race and the same language living along this border, when hundreds of thousands of United States citizens are coming to Canada and hundreds of thousands of Canadians are going over to the United States, our problem is a somewhat peculiar one. I received from one organization in the west a resolution urging that if no step could be taken to give relief by means of the Imperial conference, we should develop some sort of distinctive Canadian citizenship which would enable us to safeguard the interests of our Canadian citizens.
As a matter of fact we have developed a distinction between British citizenship and Canadian citizenship, in that, according to the United States laws, native-born Canadians may cross the international boundary without any difficulty, whereas citizens who are not Canadian-born must submit to the quota law prevailing in the United States. Hence in practice we are developing somewhat of a distinction between those two classes of our citizens. In passing I may say that if we had any national self respect in Canada, we would not allow such a distinction to continue. I do not know whether the question should be raised on this item, but I should like the minister to enlighten the committee in regard to it. My hon. friend is quite correct, and he would assist the Bureau of Statistics by furnishing a definition of what constitutes a Canadian. The statistical department is trying to compile its information on racial lines. It is a difficult question, and I think the committee would be willing to hear suggestions at the right time.
Why should there be any difficulty? Are we not proud of our. country? Are we not satisfied to call it Canada?
Is a Chinaman born in Vancouver a Canadian?	*

I am a little doubtful myself about this. I understand, although of course I could -not verify it personally, that my greatgrandfather was born in Ireland. I do not know whether anyone would ever suspect it.
There is no doubt about it.	_

On the other hand, my mother was born in the Orkney islands. Now, should I insist on telling the census enumerator that I am a Canadian, or should I say that my origin is Scotch or Irish? I should like again to draw the attention of the minister to a point that has been raised on several occasions since 1921 in regard to our manufacturing institutions filing all manner of returns with the govern-

ment which are more or less a duplication. Then a subdivision dealing with chemical and metallurgical industry will ask for practically the same particulars as have been already supplied to the census of industry. It was urged in this House in 1922, and again in 1923 and 1924f that this work should be consolidated so that business institutions would not be bothered with this duplication of returns. I am glad to be able to
tell my bon. friend that a good deal of progress has been made towards eliminating the duplication of statistics. That was primarily the idea in creating the bureau. More and more the various departments of government are centralizing their work. Not only so, but the Dominion Statistician is endeavouring to cooperate still more with the provincial governments in order to avoid the necessity of making two sets of vital statistics. I agree with my hon. friend as to the character of the returns required from manufacturing concerns -some of the statistics required by the bureau are very difficult of compilation, I took the matter up with the Dominion Statistician, and he told me that he had very little trouble in administering the act. Where he has found it work a hardship on smaller business people he has not made himself at all objectionable.
What about other departments?
Has there been any coordination with other departments?

We are working on
