I represent what may be called an extremely cosmopolitan district and the enumerators in taking the census two months ago met with a great deal of difficulty in eliciting from Ukrainians any admission that they were Ukrainians. They insisted that they were Canadians. They said, "You teach us Canadian ways and you insist on our becoming Canadians, and yet you want us to admit that we are Ukrainians." We are making ourselves most ridiculous in trie eyes of these people; we are not fair with them and I see no reason in the wide world why, during all these years, we should have continued the present anomaly. Simply because our forebears may have come from parts of the universe where we may be utterly unknown *we are bound to describe ourselves as of this and that nationality. The time has come when, as a duty to these new Canadians, we should establish a distinctly Canadian nationality.

This question is one that concerns not only the newer parts of Canada but the oldest organized sections as well. No father or mother in Ontario, or any other province, though Canadian-born, can register a child as a Canadian; it does not matter whether the parentage is Canadian for two or three generations back, unless some change is made the name "Canadian" means nothing.

During the last census this summer the Bureau of Statistics did endeavour to do some work along this line, and I believe a new definition of Canadian citizenship is now fixed. There is a regulation in this regard. The idea, I believe, is to define as a Canadian anyone bom of the third generation of natives.

Last year on two or three
occasions I interviewed the Bureau of Statistics on this question, which is one I have had under consideration for some time. We should be able to define precisely what a Canadian is. It is a lamentable fact that those of us who have to write out birth and death certificates are unable to say that a man who die3 or a child who is born is a Canadian; the certificate must give this or that nationality. It would be well to decide that anyone born in Canada should be regarded as a Canadian, and in our statistical tables there might be a special column to
[Mr. Kennedy.1
show that, with another column indicating racial origin. Certainly we should start at some' point and say what constitutes a Canadian.

I agree with my hon.
friend. In a general way there is no reason why those of us of English extraction, those of us of the white races at least, should not be called Canadians if born in Canada. When I looked into the matter, however, I appreciated the difficulties with which it bristled and with which the Census bureau must cope. It is our desire, just as it is the desire in the United States, to have some record of the number of people from foreign countries who have become Canadians. We want, for instance, to keep track of the number of Chinese in Canada, and there are Chinese and Japanese on the Pacific coast, bom of the third generation in this country.
Plow many?

I have not the figures.
I think it is just as well for us to retain this information. I have no doubt the whole subject will be found quite interesting, if any hon. member cares to look into it. It has been given a good deal of consideration and I can assure the committee that I will take the matter up with the bureau before the next census is taken in 1931.
The minister refers tc Chinese and Japanese, but he fails to appreciate the difficulty in which Canadians find themselves.
I appreciate it.

In recording the
birth of a child there is only one comprehensive definition possible, and that is Nordic. You may use that term and be perfectly safe, but you cannot call the child Irish unless both parents are full-blooded Irish. The same thing applies to Scottish people, and yet for the sake of a few Chinese and Japanese all 'our records are wrong. I do not know of any classification under which you would put a Canadian other than Nordic.

I would suggest that this subject should be discussed under a resolution. The hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) is quite right; he knows the difficulties of the 'medical profession, but that is a matter of provincial record, where the same difficulty arises as in the census record.

I think the main difficulty 'in the past has been that we had a few Indians in Canada and they would be naturally the first Canadians. At present they are all

Item agreed to.
Honorary Advisory Council for Scientific and Industrial Research, $170,000.

I desire to say a word in connection with this item. I see that this vote has been slightly increased, but I want to express my opinion to the minister that after a good deal of sympathetic study of this question I believe the amount is altogether too small. I think the time has arrived when Canada should take a definite stand on the question of establishing a bureau of standards and a fully equipped research laboratory. Members of the House will recall that about 1918 a committee of this. House made a very complete report on this subject and recommended the establishment of such plants here, similar to the Mellon Institute in the United States, in order that this great country with its remarkable opportunities and vast quantities of raw materials may bring science and industry together, as I heard one of the leading scientists of the country put it last week, and in order to derive the fullest possible advantage of the application of science to industry. It is too late to do anything this session of course, but I would like to appeal to the minister- and I know I am appealing to sympathetic ears-that during the coming recess a definite scheme should be worked out and if necessary a special bill introduced into this House- some time early in next session, in order that it may be given full consideration-providing for the establishment of such a bureau of standards and research laboratory in Canada. In this country we turn out some of

Supply-Trade and Commerce
the best educated young men in the world, hundreds of whom go to the United States when they finish their schooling here. They each cost us perhaps from $10,000 to $20,000 for their education, then they go to the United States where they enter the big industries and where they are giving wonderful service. I am told that approximately 60 per cent of the honour graduates of one university-the very cream of Canadian young manhood, and I suppose the same thing would apply to almost all our universities- find positions south of the line after they have received their schooling in this country. At the same time we have waiting for solution in this country problems which are not exceeded by those of any other country in the world. I am not offering this suggestion in a spirit of criticism at all, but rather as a wholly non-partisan matter, something which is not political but which is national in its importance. I am offering the suggestion so that next year parliament may be in possession of some definite suggestion by the government for the establishment of such a bureau here. I have in mind this: that Canada ought to vote forthwith-not this session, I presume that is impossible; when I say forthwith I mean at the earliest opportunity -say a million dollars for the establishment of a first-class, highly equipped plant here, and then give the committee a grant of say $250,000 or $300,000 a year for its operation. Of course, a moderate fee should be charged those who use the plant in any proposition which they bring to the institute for solution. Some revenue will be received, although not enough, of course, to pay the cost. I urge the minister, if he will take the suggestion from me, that perhaps the greatest service that could be rendered to Canada during the next decade would be the erection of such a plant in Ottawa, or whatever suitable place may be chosen, and I hope that next year we may have in the estimates, or in the form of a special bill, provision for such an establishment.

May I ask the
minister if he will leave this item over until after recess? It is one of the most important items in the whole estimate. I spoke a year ago on this work of a bureau of standards, and what it actually means to the manufacturer and to the consumer-more to the consumer than to the manufacturer. I should like to take the matter up in connection with the report of the research committee to-night.

I can assure my hon.
friend that I shall be pleased to leave the item over if he wishes to make any comments fMr. Stevens.]
in line with the comments made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. I know the committee will appreciate the difficulty that I as a new minister necessarily experienced in taking up any comprehensive scheme in the first few months I was in charge of the department.
Quite.

May I say that I am
entirely sympathetic towards the idea. I do not believe that we have expended in Canada anything like the amount of money we might on industrial research, or even on agricultural research. There is a slight increase in the vote this year, and there will likely be an increase in the supplementaries for some work that is being arranged for. I shall be delighted indeed to hear and to consider any comments favourable to the work that hon. members wish to make in committee.

this would be the proper place to announce what is being done in Montreal. Not only should we do that, but we should utilize the services of every university in Canada, as is done now under the scientific research bureau, and thus bring into play all those activities that will mean so much for the development of science and industry in this country and will perhaps, as my hon. friend has said, provide employment for a great many more of our young men who take this special training.

I wish to say a word in
support of this proposal to increase our research facilities in Canada, having in mind particularly that phase of the question which has reference to the contagious diseases of animals and the necessity of pathological research along these lines, so as to obviate the great loss from which we suffer in this coum

Supply-Trade and Commerce
try from these diseases, and effect a large saving in the compensation which has to be paid. I wish to commend the government for the construction of a large pathological laboratory near Hull, which is a step in the right direction. A few years ago we had an outbreak of disease amongst horses in the province of Saskatchewan, and in one year we paid $47,000 in compensation. The gentleman in charge out there at that time, having his headquarters at Lethbridge, was Dr. Watson, now the head of the pathological laboratory across the river. Dr. Watson was able to discover a blood test which he applied to these horses so as to diagnose the disease before the ordinary symptoms appeared. In about six years, by carrying on work along this line, he reduced the amount of compensation paid from $47,000 to $300, and the next year to $70. Since then nothing at all has been paid. Thus this work resulted in a complete saving to the country and it is only a little illustration of what it is possible to do along this line. I think that everyone who has the good of Canada at heart, and realizes to anything like a full extent the wonderful opportunities for research work in this country, will stand strongly behind any policy brought down by the government which has that object in view.

pictures.

The deputy minister, of course, at times has to go away on different duties in connection with the department, and it has been found necessary to have an assistant deputy minister.
What is his name?

F. C. Blair. There are three divisions, eastern, middle and western, and the commissioner of immigration has charge of 'the different divisions. The commissioner of colonization is in charge of the different activities of his department.

We know the
definition of colonization. What are the commissioner's duties?

He has charge of the work
of placing farm labourers in positions and locating farmers.
I presume he would act between immigrants guaranteed positions and applicants for farm help.
Yes.

Where does the
work of the commissioner of immigration end and that of the commissioner of colonization begin?

The commissioner of immigration is directly interested in attracting immigrants, which necessitates his keeping in touch with all the overseas offices of his department. The commissioner of colonization is more particularly interested in immigrants after their arrival here.
Is not the Soldier Settlement Board now really a colonization board? And does this item include the staff of that board?
There is a separate estimate for the Soldier Settlement Board.
The colonization branch?

There is a land settlement
branch in connection with the Soldier Settlement Board, which is a distinct branch, although the two work in unison.

Supply-Immigration

Is there a division of work, the land settlement board looking after certain settlers and the commissioner of colonization looking after others? To an outsider there seems to be a good deal of overlapping in this department.

There is no overlapping,
although of course they may be brought in touch with each other occasionally in the course of their work. The land settlement board is more particularly concerned with the three thousand family scheme for the settling of British farmers, and other schemes. The officials are really connected with the Soldier Settlement Board.

Could not all the work of
the land settlement board and the Soldier Settlement Board be handled to much better advantage under the one department?

They are under the Department of Immigration and Colonization, although at the present time there are three commissioners of the Soldier Settlement Board. Ultimately I hope to bring them all directly under the control of my department. I have no complaints on the score of efficiency, but I do think it would be better to have these two branches of the service under one control.
Hear, hear.

It seems to me that probably for the past three years the Soldier Settlement Board has been engaged in straight colonization work. I know a great many people are asking why we need that board to carry on virtually the same work as the department of colonization. One department ought to be sufficient.

I would point out to the
hon. member that the land settlement board and the Soldier Settlement Board have practically the same officials. The supervisors of the Soldier Settlement Board look after soldier settlers and also after farmers who have come to us under the three thousand family scheme; in fact they supervise all the activities in connection with colonization. There is no overlapping, for the Department of Immigration has no officials doing that particular kind of work. Undoubtedly those officials are very helpful in placing settlers on farms and looking after them for a few years.

Is it too much to expect
that in the next year or two we shall be able to get along with fewer commissioners? The
minister said there Tvere three in the Soldier Settlement Board, and two are mentioned in this list. To an outsider five commissioners to look after our colonization work is suggestive of overstaffing.

I should not like to say
that. Of course,.when we come to the Soldier Settlement Board it will be a matter of legitimate criticism as to whether it is the best possible organization for the work it handles. It must be borne in mind that I have not yet had time to become thoroughly familiar with the ramifications of my department, which extend not only throughout the Dominion but all over the United States and in many of the countries of Europe. In fact, we are in touch with every civilized country in the world. So far I see no reason to believe that these officials are not absolutely necessary. We have a commissioner for the eastern division who certainly has to cover a very large field, and the same remark applies to the commissioner of the central and western divisions. In fact, these and other men have a great deal more work to attend to than those outside the department would imagine.
Does this item refer only to the Ottawa officials?
Yes.
Has the minister the information as to the number of juvenile immigrants brought in during the past year? Or would he rather deal with this under another item?
There were 975 brought to Ontario.
All from Britain?
Yes. The department gives after-care to a great many of the boys brought out, and it is a part of the duties of the commissioner to see to that.
It is impossible for us over here to hear what is being said. This seems to be a private conversation.
There were brought out to the country last year in all 1470 boys, 975 of whom came to Ontario.

In connection with juvenile work the minister seems to have come into collision with the Salvation Army. Will he explain why he has taken such a stand against the work of the Salvation Army?

I cannot very well answer that question because I deny having taken any such stand. If hon. gentlemen cannot hear me perhaps it is because of my Scotch accent.
There is no need to laugh. This is an interesting question and I have a right to hear what the minister says.
There is no need to insult the minister.

If the Minister of
Railways will come and sit over here he will see how difficult it is for us to hear.
I will do my best to make myself heard.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would ask hon. members to keep better order.

I am anxious to give any information I can regarding the subject. I can assure my hon. friends that it is no laughing matter to me. I am quite serious at this moment. I think all hon. gentlemen will appreciate the statement that I have no inclination just now to be facetious or to indulge in humour. I do not agree with the suggestion that I have shown any antagonism towards the Salvation Army.

The public press discloses beyond any possibility of doubt that there is a serious difference of opinion between the minister or his department and the officers of the Salvation Army. We want to know what are the causes of difference and what the minister has done to meet the situation satisfactorily.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Every hon. member knows
that when a minister is putting through his estimates he has prepared an outline of the work which he follows consecutively. I think we should get along much better and my colleague (Mr. Forke) would be in a more advantageous position to answer questions if we were to dispose of civil government first and then, in connection with the votes for the various societies, discuss questions in relation thereto.

A question was
raised regarding juvenile work and in all seriousness I have asked for information. It seemed to me as though the minister were regarding the matter as a joke.
Not at all.

Immediately I
ask for information hon. gentlemen opposite

take me up. I am here for information and I am prepared to stay until I get it. What I want to know is quite relevant to the matter.

If not under this item, will the minister indicate where we may discuss the general immigration policy of the department?
RORKE: It may be discussed under immigration contingencies," which covers the^ whole field. But I have no objection to giving now any information in regard to juvenile work. I have here a long explanation which I do not consider it necessary to read. Coming into the department a few months ago, I was not very well acquainted with the various activities of the Salvation Army, but so far as I am concerned the first friction with that organization arose out of the fact that the Salvation Army was collecting a part of the. transportation fees which had already been paid by the imperial and the federal governments. Hon. gentlemen have no doubt seen the explanations given by Commissioner Lamb regarding that statement. The Salvation Army received a grant, of S25,000 for carrying on immigration work, and that seemed reasonable so long as no other organization was engaged in the same field. I found however, that there were ten or fifteen or more organizations, all anxious to assist in immi-gation work and all seeking grants from the Dominion government. It was impossible to give grants to all these organizations, who are doing bona fide work in furthering immigration, and the only thing for it was to cut out direct grants to any immigration association. ^ The Salvation Army felt hurt but this decision, I can assure the committee, was dictated by no antagonism whatever to the organization in question. It was purely a matter of policy, and I do not think that either the Salvation Army or any other association can possibly find fault with the department for taking such a step.
With regard to juvenile immigration, I may observe that, boys under seventeen are brought over free of charge, whether they come out to institutions devoted to the welfare of Boys, or to any of the provincial organizations. The Dominion government pays fifty per cent and the imperial government the other fifty. More than that, the federal government makes a grant to the farm-such as the Yimy farm in Ontario-of $20 for each boy while the provincial government contributes a like sum. The imperial government makes a grant of S40.

Supply-Immigration
To whom?

Either to the Ontario government or to the particular organization under w'hose control the boys may be. We are trying to establish farms in all the provinces, and the work is being taken up. The Salvation Army has exactly the some opportunities as any other organization. Apart from the wdthdrawal of the grant, the first trouble that arose in connection with the army was due to the fact that, although the transportation fees were being paid by the imperial and federal governments, the Salvation Army was collecting money from the boys after they had come to Canada. Their statement was that before leaving Great Britain the boys agreed to pay a certain sum to the Army in order that other iboys should have the same advantages, while quite a number of boys came here and they said that when they signed the document they were under the impression that they were repaying the Salvation Army for their passage money. I am not making any charge against the Salvation Army, but I do say the boys were under a misapprehension, and in speaking to Commissioner Lamb I think I told him that I knew something of what it meant for a boy to come out here and work for a farmer for $10 a month Commissioner Lamb said the boy would get $20 a month, but I wonder where boys fifteen and sixteen years of age are being paid $20 a month on farms? They get about $10 a month, and when the Salvation Army collected some of that money, and perhaps most of it, there was not much left. The arrangement was that the farmer would pay the money direct to the Salvation Army, that the boy would not get it at all, and I still think this gave the boy a bad start; in many cases it might cause him to lose heart and (become a failure without having had a fair chance. I know that Commissioner Lamb will not agree with what I am saying, but I have had some practical experience in dealing with boys, perhaps more than he has had. That wras the whole trouble, and I do not know of anything other than that. The Salvation Army has the same opportunities and the same privileges accorded other organizations, and we are willing to cooperate with them in just the same way. I am sorry Commissioner Lamb got into the newspapers, because I do not think it did either the department or the Salvation Army any good. I have tried to make the situation as plain as I can and I think roughly that covers the whole case.

I would like to ask the minister a question in that connection. I understand that he objects to the Salvation Army having any private arrangement with the boy who comes out under their auspices, to the effect that he will pay back a certain sum to the army in the course of a certain length of time. My understanding is that this is an arrangement or agreement between the Salvation Army officials and the immigrant boy, and I cannot look upon it as the minister does. I do not think it is a handicap to the boy; to the contrary, I think it makes him feel that he is doing something worth while in assisting to bring another boy to the country wdiere he has found employment.
Let us consider the statement of the minister. He says it is wrong for the Salvation Army to make an arrangement with a boy immigrant whereby that boy agrees to pay a certain sum of money to the Salvation Army to assist in bringing out another boy. Let us take the case of a man coming to Canada from Italy, let us say, or some other part of continental Europe. It is a fact, as the minister must know, that there are organizations in this country which put up money for that immigrant to show when he lands here, in order to prove that he is not a pauper. That money is turned back to that organization when he lands here within a certain period of time, by arrangement; then the money is used to bring out another person. What about that principle?
I have no knowledge of any such thing.

My hon. friend can say that he has only been in the department a short time, and we will accept that excuse for his want of knowledge. But let me tell him something further. There is a well-established organization in New York with a branch right in Ottawa which brings immigrants to this country. Supposing I make a representation, or some other member of this House makes a representation, to the minister to allow a certain immigrant to enter this country to work on a farm. I get my permit and go to the agent of this New York company in Ottawa and say, "Here is a permit for an immigrant." He will give me a cheque on the bank in Ottawa for $50 for each immigrant I get in in that way. Does the minister not know of that fact, that there are people in this country who are simply taking the voters' list or the telephone directory, writing out a list of names and
Supply-Immigration

getting permits from the department to bring immigrants into this country, which permits are turned into cash by presenting them to the agent of this New York organization? Does he not know that there is a well-established underground channel for conveying info the United States those immigrants who, for obvious reasons, do not want to stay in Canada? There is a systematized organization at work getting men into Canada under these false representations and then smuggling them across the line. It is all very well to say that this does not happen often, but will the minister tell me that he is not aware of the fact that there are firms right here in Canada- one in the city of Toronto whose name just escapes me for the moment

which put up the money and which have banking arrangements in Europe, so that the immigrant from that continent can say he is not a pauper? The company makes an arrangement with him and he not only pays back the amount they put up for him to make good in entering this country, but he has to pay as well a mighty good commission. Then that money is used again to bring in other immigrants in the same way; they have a complete organization, with a banking system on the continent of Europe and with agents here in Canada. That is going on now and has been going on for some time- The minister says that is all right; he does not object to that, but if the Salvation Army sees fit to enter into a private arrangement with a boy whom they bring to this country, in order that he may assist them in the work they are carrying on by paying back to the Salvation Army a certain amount of money in a certain time, the minister finds that objectionable.

When I said I did not know anything about this, perhaps I did not exactly state the case, although I was speaking truthfully in one respect. I can assure the hon. member that this has been one of the great sources of trouble to me since I took over this department; it came upon me like a clap of thunder, because I never assumed that any such operations were being carried on. I have no doubt that it is being done, but every attempt of which I become aware will receive no favour and no consideration from me as Minister of Immigration. I think perhaps it is nothing like as bad as the hon. member seems to think, but I do not intend to do anything in my position as Minister of Immigration which will not stand investigation, and I hope to be able to face this House at any time and say I have done what I thought was right, and face any criticism which may result. 
I will make mistakes and blunders, but I want the House to know that no hon. member will ever find me entering into any arrangements of any kind which are not upright and honourable in every way.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Would my
hon. friend explain how the door is closed against immigrants from the old land?

I did not
say that the door was closed against them.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
At any rate
you said it was made difficult for them to enter.

Yes, it is
made difficult for them to enter. Here is an instance in regard to the Salvation Army where I think the government have been too strict, where they have drawn the line rather tight, in shutting out immigrants who are admittedly of the class we want to get in this country.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We are not
shutting out Britishers.

I think we
have been too strict in regard to the immigrant boys brought out by the Salvation Army.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
They were
not shut out.
I did not say they were Shut out. I said the immigration of these boys was restricted and discouraged.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.

If jTou do
not call it discouragement, what do you call it-encouragement ?

The Salvation Army boys are getting exactly the same chance as any other immigrants. At the present moment they are under no disabilities whatever. May I explain that the Salvation Army was getting a grant of $25,000 a year for its immigration and colonization work? As I tried to explain at the outset we were giving all the after-care that was necessary in regard to the immigrants that were coming in because I take this position-that no matter what organization is engaged in immigration work the department is responsible, in the final analysis, for the immigrants that come to this country. I say frankly that I do not want to transfer my responsibility to any organization. Now the Salvation Army boys are getting the same chance as others. In the matter of transportation they come across free, the federal and imperial governments still pay the passage money, but now we give no $25,000 a year grant. We give the same treatment to the Salvation Army that is accorded, for example, to the Vimy Ridge organization. I am very sorry indeed that this matter with respect to the Salvation Army ever got into the newspapers. But for that there would have been no talk whatever about any antagonism between the department and the Salvation Army. I have a great admiration for the Salvation Army, and if I may be permitted to say so I have contributed every year out of my small resources toward the work that the Army is carrying on. This matter need never have been [DOT] ventilated as it has been. Personally I think the Salvation Army made a mistake in getting into the newspapers and making a noise about a matter as to which they really have no grievance.
Did the minister cut off the grant of $25,000 a year?
No.
Is the grant continued to the Salvation Army?
It is finished now.
I see, you have cut off the grant.
I endeavoured to explain that there are church organizations, societies of all kinds, entering into immigration work. They all want some assistance. It may have been a mistake, I do not know-
How long have the Salvation Army been getting this special grant of $25,000?

I could not tell you.
Supply-Immigration
Your deputy can tell you in a moment.
My deputy informs me that they have been getting a grant of a certain amount for about thirty years, but it never assumed any large proportion until five years ago.
Now it is cut off.
It is cut off, yes.

I have a deep appreciation of the situation in which the minister finds himself, and I am not inclined to be hypercritical about his course but rather in the greatest degree friendly. My understanding of the case is that the Salvation Army spend a good deal of money upon these boys before they ever leave the old country. The Army maintain training farms or stations which cost them a great deal of money. Now what they do, as I am informed, is this: they collect from the boys a certain sum, but that is not equal to the amount they spend on them before they start for this country. It is not the passage money that the boys repay; it is the money that is expended in preparing them to be citizens in Canada. I hope the minister will reconsider his decision, and that he will restore the grant to the Salvation Army.

I want to explain before
going any further that the $25,000 was not a grant made in connection with the boys; it was a grant for the general immigration work of the organization.

No matter how the grant may be viewed by the department, if one studies broadly the work of the Salvation Army I think he will admit that there is no organization engaged in immigration work, trying to get good British citizens into Canada, that is quite as efficient as the Salvation Army. Needing population as we do and the Salvation Army being chiefly concerned in bringing out younger people, the very kind of people we want,-and I remember receiving applause from this side of the House one session when I suggested that boys rather than mature people should be brought out-I think the work which the Salvation Anmy are doing and endeavouring to do is the best that can be done. Why not encourage them to do that work? If there is any other organization that will undertake the same responsibilities and bring us the same class of citizens, why not give them a grant? If any other organization in England has a training depot to prepare boys for life in Canada, that work entails a 
heavy expense and it should be encouraged. Giving assistance in that way is much better than picking up boys in this or that town or some other part of Great Britain and bringing them out to Canada without any sorting out and without any training. My information is that many boys who are taken in hand by the Salvation Army for immigration to Canada are not sent out to this country because, during the period of training, the army discover that this or that boy is not likely to make good and so they do not send him out to us. They send out only those boys who, during the period of training, have shown that they are likely to become good citizens of Canada. I hope the minister will reconsider this matter and that this policy which he has adopted will be, to say the least, somewhat modified. Let him give the Salvation Army a liberal grant, and let him give a proportionate grant to any other organization that is doing work of the same character. Surely that is the best thing that can be done for the promotion of immigration of good quality to this country. Will the minister change his policy?

I would not like at the present time to make any promise, because I want to reiterate that the Salvation Army is receiving exactly the same treatment as that accorded to other organizations which are dealing with boys. The department is giving them the $10 grant for every boy they train on their farm in England, and we are willing to pay, along with the Imperial government, one-half of the transportation charges. That involves a large amount of money when you figure it out for every boy coming to this country.
How much does the Army pay?
The Army pays nothing for transportation. We are willing to give them the $10 grant for training the boy on the other side.
That will not pay the cost of training.
No. The British government is paying $20.
That will buy only a suit of clothes.

We are willing to pay them the $10 and we give the boys free transportation across the ocean. It is easy for hon. members to talk, but if you figure what the cost to the Dominion is, for all these boys you will find that you are not going to have

Supply-I mini gra tion
many $25,000 grants to give to organizations throughout the country. There seems to be an impression that the Salvation Army is being discriminated against. The hon. member for Toronto West Centre speaks of the importance of their work. I have nothing to say against the Salvation Army, but there are other organizations doing just as good work.
And maintaining training depots in the old country?

That have training depots
in the old country.

What other organization
is doing that?
Mr. FORKE,: They do not have training farms, but they are doing training work. We have the Ontario government entering into this work on the Vimy ridge farm in connection with, the Dominion government. The Manitoba government, the New Brunswick government and the Nova Scotia government are going to go into this work and we are making the same grants to all these boys. The total amount of money paid out in assisting immigration of this character will be considerable. This is not being done in a spirit of antagonism to the Salvation Army. I criticized their collection of money from these boys; as a practical fanner I did not think it was a wise policy to adopt. But that is only a matter of opinion; I am not condemning the Army for doing that.

Did the department not
issue a statement to the press that if the Army continued that practice the grant would be discontinued? I recall seeing in the press some time ago an apparently inspired statement to that effect. That is what has created the protest against the special treatment meted out to the Salvation Army. I am inclined to think the training which the New Brunswick government proposes to give to these boys is on this side of the water and not on the other.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
There is a
good deal of misconception about the position that is now taken as against that formerly taken by the department. Prior to the inception of the assisted passage scheme, grants were given to societies which engaged in this work. I increased the Salvation Army grant from $15,000 to $25,000, believing that the Army was a fair medium for this class of work. But the Baroardo home has been bringing boys to Canada for years and a number of patriotic associations have been doing the same thing.
Is the Barnardo home still doing that?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Yes. There are various organizations bringing out boys. My hon. friends will remember when in 1923,
I think, we began the assisted passage scheme for boys from fourteen to seventeen years of age. Part of the passage was paid by the Imperial government and part by this government, and their transportation was absolutely free. There was no charge to any of these organizations for bringing the boys over. It was felt then that we might very well cut off the grants that were being earned by these various organizations which were engaged in this business of bringing in juvenile immigrants. The reason for that was that they were receiving from the two governments, under the assisted passage scheme, assistance which they never received before.
I am not familiar with the controversy that may have arisen over the Salvation Army; but if we are to give in a larger way than any $25,000 grant in assisting the Salvation Army to bring boys to this country, I do not see 'much necessity for continuing these grants. I am much interested in the attempt to work in harmon}' with the provincial government because this will prevent overlapping in organizations. Let the provincial government assume the responsibility of placing all immigrants, not only the juveniles but the adults as well. I tried that when I first became minister of the department. I went right across Canada, interviewed every provincial government, and said to them that if they would undertake the colonization of the immigrants who came into their province, we would be willing to pay our fair proportion of the cost of those immigrants, believing that the provincial government would have the best knowledge of and facilities for doing this work. I was however unable at the time to get the provinces to agree to that. They said: This is the business of the federal government; they ought not only to recruit immigrants, but to place them when they come into this country. I was unable to make that arrangement but I still think it is the ideal one.
Let the federal government provide an organization for the recruiting of those-children as well as adults-who may foe required by the various provinces; let the federal government meet the expense of colonization; but let the work be assumed by the provincial government. My colleague is doing that in connection with juvenile immigration as far as it can be done, in an attempt to get away froni these organizations some of which have been engaged in this work and some of
Supply-Immigration

which want to go into it. I realize the difficulty in dealing with these organizations. This is no sinecure for any minister. I am still convinced that I was right in 1922, and if we are going to have a real immigration policy in Canada, it is the only one that will work out successfully and the one that will cost the least.
That is not the policy which the minister followed.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The reason was that with the exception of making arrangements with the provinces for juveniles, I was unable to arrive at an agreement.
The minister under the grant gave assisted passages to those brought out by the Salvation Army and he raised no objection in connection with the matter.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Not when
I raised the grant to the Salvation Army.
I understand the Minister of the Interior to say that the Barnardo home is bringing out children now. Will he confirm that?

They are not bringing very
many.
Any at all?
Oh, yes.

Is there no regulation
forbidding the bringing out of these children?

Under fourteen years of
age. There was an investigation made into the circumstances connected with the immigration of boys under fourteen years of age. After that investigation Margaret Bondfield came to Canada; her verdict was against boys of_ that- age coming to Canada, and the immigration of boys of that age has been largely stopped. Very few are coming out unless to some special home.
I think it is peculiarand I am not referring to the present minister now, because this was done before he took office-that the Department of Immigration should take the word of Miss Bond-field-
Oh, no.
That is what the minister said.

Almost every child welfare
society in the country was objecting to the immigration of children under fourteen years of age.

The experience in this
country will prove that we have had no better immigration to Canada than the immigration from the Barnardo home. Here and there it has been discovered that a boy did not make good, but taking the matter by and large the Barnardo home has done more good work for Canada in proportion to its opportunities and funds than any organization I know of. I am not blaming the minister, but the department does not believe that children under that age should come out. I disagree entirely with that view, and I disagree entirely with the argument that was used that a child should not come to Canada until he has received a public school education in England. If a child of five or six comes to Canada and is educated here he has a better chance of making good than if he is brought out at the age of fourteen or fifteen. I think no greater mistake has ever been made in the administration of this department than the prohibiting of the Barnardo home from carrying on the work it had performed for about fourteen years. Thousands of men who hold good positions in this country came out under the auspices of that organization. They have made good; some of them are wealthy men and are now contributing their funds to assist the organization which brought them out here. I think the department should cancel that regulation and permit the Barnardo home to use the same judgment that they have used for so many years in bringing children to this country.
The Salvation Army are bringing out a lot of immigrants. They get their passage money and are given, I think, $30 by the federal government and the Imperial government. That $30 does not pay for their training in the old country. An organization such as the Salvation Army, with its little groups and stations in practically every community in Canada, is in a better position to do good work in the matter of immigration than any other body. I see no reason why the Salvation Army should be forced to spend the money it has collected from other sources and for other purposes in the work of assisting immigration to Canada. I do not believe the $25,000 grant they have been receiving would by any means pay for what the}'- spend upon the emigrants before they leave the other side. It is not fair to ask the Salvation Army to use their funds to advance immigration. They have given us the benefit of their widespread organizations, and they keep track 'of every immigrant who comes out under their auspices. It is a splendid organization and I think it would be a reasonable thing for the government to

Supply-Immigration
pay this $25,000. If there is any other organization doing the same kind of work .and doing it as well as the Salvation Army why not pay that organization as well? Each society or organization which is concerned in immigration should be dealt with on its merits; there should not be a blanket regulation placed over all. Some are doing well and some not so well, but each should be tested by its accomplishment and treated with some degree of sympathy, not merely to show that we recognize their good work but also to encourage them in future.
What other organizations have received grants of this kind, and how much in each case?

While the minister is finding the answer to that question, I want to back him up in the cutting off of grants to different societies. If we are going to carry on the work of immigration let us do it ourselves. Let us spend the money on the people we want, and not hand it over to these societies.

What amount is appropriated for the maritime provinces? We all know that in the past the maritime provinces have suffered in this respect; they have not received the amount of assistance which they deserve. In 1923 the railway department amalgamated the various amounts spent in the various provinces under the colonization scheme, and it is practically impossible to determine what is spent in each province. What does the minister propose to do in connection with the expenditure by his department in the maritime provinces? Judging by the legislation which has been brought down as a result of the Duncan report, it has become very apparent that in Canada to-day we need a broad east and west policy, not only for immigration and for railways, but for other departments. The time has arrived for the government to recognize this important matter and in determining their various expenditures throughout Canada to size up the situation from the east to the west and from the north to the south. It is time for the government to realize that the people of Canada expect something which will bring about a real consciousness of nationalization in this country. We want something which will tend to bring about a better feeling among the people from coast to coast. Let the Minister of Immigration tell us what he proposes to do in regard to expenditures in the maritime provinces.

During the few months that I have been in the department I have recognized that, if colonization and immigration
are to be successful, the cooperation of the people of the whole country must be had. I look upon immigrants as wards of this department. It is our duty to see that they get a fair "chance. This can only be done effectively by individuals and communities and the provincial governments entering into cooperation with the Dominion authorities. We have in the west what are known as community building clubs, and they are of inestimable benefit in helping new immigrants. They meet the new arrivals, encourage them, give them advice and make them feel at home. I say again to the maritime provinces: You too have got to help; the Immigration department cannot do it alone. I am anxious that something shall be done for the maritime provinces not only as recommended by the Duncan report but in the way of immigration and colonization.
Something of real value.

Yes. We are ready to enter into negotiations with the Nova Scotia and New Brunswick governments. I was in error in saying that we have an arrangement with New Brunswick for boy immigrants; the arrangement is in relation to the three thousand family scheme. We have an arrangement with Nova Scotia for boy immigrants. They are taking one hundred boys this year as a start, working in cooperation with my department. We are willing to enter into the same arrangement with New Brunswick-in fact, as I said before, with all the provinces.
As to settling immigrants on some of the vacant lands in the maritime provinces, I find it rather a difficult proposition. Out of surplus funds in connection with the three thousand family soheme, the government has tried to get options on some vacant farms. Wherever we can get British families assisted by a loan of three hundred pounds from the Imperial government to settle on farms in the maritime provinces we are ready to proceed. But let me say again, we must have provincial cooperation if our efforts are to be successful. I do not want to see those people lose heart at the outset by being told that they cannot make a living on farms in the maritime provinces. I have seen some of those farms, and as a farmer I say that I would not be afraid to go down there and make a living. I do not see why British farmers could not do the same. I am willing and anxious to do all I can to help the maritime provinces secure immigrants, but I ask for cooperation by the provincial governments of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. So far I have found them willing to help me in this work.

Then I understand the minister has not yet made any actual arrangement with the governments of the maritime provinces; he simply expresses his willingness to do so.
Oh yes.

I understand that Mr. Murray, the gentleman in charge of immigration work in New Brunswick, has gone to the old country. Has he made any arrangement with the minister's department with respect to this work? If so, what is it? We can only assimilate a certain number of people in my province at the beginning, but there should be no difficulty, if the organization is perfected, in making it possible to bring out families under the British government scheme and place them on small holdings in New Brunswick. They should be able to make a living there very easily from the beginning if they have had any training at all. I rather sympathize with the view of the present Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) that the provinces ought to help in this immigration work, because at very little expense they can create the necessary machinery to place farmers on the land, and especially boys. There ought to be cooperation and coordination not only between the federal and provincial departments, but between the railways and the provincial and Dominion governments. I believe there 'is some such working arrangement already in effect. I think the minister will find the present government in New Brunswick sympathetic towards any scheme of immigration that he may propose to them. The scope of their ability to place men on the land at the beginning may be limited, but they want immigrants, and the minister will find the premier willing and ready to cooperate in any scheme that his deputy minister may propose, to a limited degree at the beginning, but gradually growing, as we all hope, to larger proportions.
While I am on my feet I should like to know if there is any contractual arrangement between the Department of Immigration and Dr. Cossar. I have known him for several years, and I 'believe him to be a real philanthropist. He came out to New Brunswick, bought one of the best farms at Gagetown, and placed in charge a competent man to train boys to become farmers. So far as I am aware only one boy of the large number that he has brought out has failed, and I have kept pretty close tab on the work done there. It has been a real success, but only on a very small scale. Dr. Cossar
fMr. Forke.]
is not making any money out of the scheme; he is simply assisting boys in the old country to become farmers, and I would bespeak for him the mosit favourable consideration of the officials of the department. I understand the minister is going to the old country this summer, and I would suggest that before he embarks he take an opportunity of calling on Dr. Cossar to see if he cannot continue the arrangement made some years ago whereby the doctor brought out boys and trained them on his farm at h'is own expense with little or no assistance except from other philanthropic persons in the old country.

Dr. Cossar brought out
seventy-eight boys last year, and I am informed by the department that he is doing splendid work. We have a working arrangement with the New Brunswick government. We are in negotiation with them for a sort of three-way arrangement between the Imperial government, the federal Department of Immigration and the provincial government, but it is not in such shape that I can give it to the House. I think it is a good arrangement.

Does Dr. Cossar get any
assistance in his work?
The boys get the regular grant for transportation.

I would ask the member for York-Sunbury or the minister, or both of them, to tell us how they expect farmers from England to make a success of farming in New Brunswick if the New Brunswick people themselves cannot do so.

Anybody with any gumption in New Brunswick is doing something. If the hon. gentleman will come down to the province I will show him in the county of York the most contented people on the face of the earth.

Mr. Chairman, people in the maritime provinces are so busy filling various offices in western and central Canada that possibly they have not had time to attend to their duties at home. Farmers in the maritime provinces are doing fairly well, but I would point out that we have been handicapped down there, we have not enjoyed the opportunities of the other portions of the Dominion. For instance, the railway department is very anxious indeed to sell a long route ticket from the old country to a point in the Dominion as far west as possible. No attempt is made to detain these people or to give them an opportunity of looking ove'1

the possibilities of the maritime provinces. If immigrants from the old country after spending some time in the prairie provinces become dissatisfied and want to come east, the railways do not give them the benefit of excursion rates such as are extended to people going west from central Canada. The Minister of Railways will bear me out when I say that from Winnipeg and points further west the rate in the summer months to the coast is reduced by something like $21.50; but if immigrants who have spent some time in the west want to come east to explore our territory they are given the munificent reduction of $1.05. This class of immigrants, the shore farmers who could make a success of shore farming in the maritime provinces, are not allowed to explore the possibilities of that section of Canada. That I think is a sufficient answer to the hon. gentleman who asked the question.
Members from the maritime provinces are practically silent just now. Let me assure the committee that we are waiting to see what will be done in connection with the Duncan report. We want to see what is to be given us. We are reserving our criticism and when the time comes we shall be quite capable of replying to hon. gentlemen in the far corner of the chamber who are just now so critical of the terms of the Duncan report. What was laid down by the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen as the remedy for conditions in the maritime provinces-the extension of the Intercolonial railway into Montreal, and development in the Atlantic region, that section of the road going to Portland-has not been taken notice of. That policy has not been carried out.	[DOT]
