I submit that we are discussing immigration estimates and not maritime rights.
The point is ridiculous.

I have not bored this House with such lengthy criticisms as some of those who at this moment would like to interrupt me have indulged in. I say that the policy laid down by the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen
32648-127i
-and I am not getting away from the immigration question-with regard to conditions in the maritime provinces, has not been carried out. So far as the maritime legislation introduced by the government at this session is concerned, we are willing, at least I am, to give the government credit for having to some extent complied with the recommendations of the Duncan report. If we have been successful in getting from the government some concessions the Duncan report has been very largely responsible for it, because the government of the day was committed to the recommendations of that commission, and the Prime Minister was committed to it. And the report gives only a faint idea of what we would have received had the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen been returned to power.

Some time ago I asked
the minister for information regarding a matter which has been the subject of considerable discussion in the newspapers. He dealt with it, at some length, but I submit that he has hardly been fair with the House. From the correspondence that appeared in the press the public was led to understand that the Salvation Army, under their working agreement with the Immigration department had not played quite squarely, and were asking boys to pledge themselves to return after they had come out to this country or as soon as they were able to do so, certain sums which it wras represented in the press had been advanced by the government. The public were also given to understand that the minister had taken the attitude that the Salvation Army could not enter into agreements of that kind with the boys and that in consequence of that opinion the army were forced to withdraw from immigration work in cooperation with the government. I understand from the reply given by Commissioner Lamb that the Salvation Army, in addition to the amount they received' from this government by way of assistance to immigration work, have spent large sums of money in the aggregate on boys coming into this country. That money has been devoted to the education of the boys in various ways and particularly to the procuring of their outfit. The boys before coming to Canada were asked to sign an agreement to return to the Salvation Army, when and as they were able to do so, such moneys as had been spent on their outfit and possibly part of their upkeep prior to their arrival here. The minister did not make that clear. I ask him now whether he considers that a fair statement of the situation, on the part, of Commissioner Lamb, and, if it is, whether he thinks there is anything wrong in
Supply-Immigration

the Salvation Army taking such a course? The minister gave the House to understand that it was a matter of opinion. Well, if it is only a matter of opinion that is hardly good enough ground on which to base such an order as was made in this matter. I know of no better way in which you can help boys to become independent men later on than by enabling them to pay their way. Let us make it possible for every one of these boys later on to say, "I paid back all that was spent on me prior to coming to Canada. I am independent of any man. I paid my way, I am not a pauper owing any organization in the world. I stand on my own feet." If the minister persists in the course he 'has taken I think he is making a mistake. I ask him now for a (dear declaration of policy in this matter. So far he has not given it.

I thought I had explained
the matter as fully as I could. I did not think that any statement had been made which I had not tried to answer. The Salvation Army takes the boys to its farm in. England and gives them probably six weeks' training. They get a grant from t'he imperial government of $20.

Is not that a
bonus?

It is a straight grant for
training. This department is willing to give $10 also for every one of these boys. That is a standing offer. This $30 is to look after these boys for six weeks. There is no doubt that many of these people are doing voluntary work which exceeds that $30 and for which they should be given credit.
My deputy informs me that the British government also makes a contribution.
That is not an answer to my question.

I am trying to answer it.
The British government also makes a contribution towards outfitting the boys. I do not want to do any double twisting at all; I want to answer every question as fairly as I can. The Imperial government and the federal government pay the cost of the passage of these boys across the ocean, and there is no discrimination against the Salvation Army in any way that I can see. We are ready to
I Mr. Cantley.]
put up a lot of money if the Salvation Army take advantage of the offers made in regard to these boys. A great deal has been said about the statements that were issued in this matter and I would like to read the only statement put out by the department.
Was this statement issued prior to the statement of Commissioner Lamb?

Commissioner Lamb made a statement purporting to be a letter issued from the office in Montreal, if I remember rightly, and that is the first time the matter got into the papers. We made no statement until Commissioner Lamb issued that letter.
I want to make it clear, because I have some remarks to make later. Did the department make their statement first?

Not in the public press;
there was a private arrangement made and negotiations were carried on in my office, but no statement appeared in the public press until Commissioner Lamb made that statement by releasing a letter from Montreal. I was sorry Commissioner Lamb released that statement, because he placed the matter before the public when there was no need for it. I have no hard feelings against the Salvation Army-I feel that I would be on the most friendly terms with Commissioner Lamb if he were here-but I think the public are making the most of it.
What was the substance of that letter released to the press? Will the minister read it?

It was a statement of their side of the case, that they were doing a splendid work and were taking care of these boys for a number of years after they came to Canada, It was his explanation in regard to the money being collected from the boys. I do not recall all that was in that letter but I believe that pretty well covers it.

Was it not a simple statement that the arrangements between the department and the Salvation Army were broken? Then the department issued a statement which was followed by another statement by Commissioner Lamb in detail, to which the minister now objects.

I do not recall that; I
think what I have stated to the House covers the whole question just as fairly as I can possibly give it from memory. I have a state-

Supply-Immigration
ment here contained in a letter written to Commissioner Lamb just before he went away, with regard to the negotiations which were being carried on. I will read the paragraph which deals with these boys.
The department will not consent to your making collections from boys of this class for reasons which have been fully explained. We have found that these boys almost without exception, believe they are refunding transportation loans provided by the Salvation Army. It makes no difference whether the collection is regarded as a refund of a loan or as a contribution to the cost of the Army's immigration machinery in Canada. No other society bringing boys to Canada requires either refund or contribution and the practice of collecting is unsettling to the boys and means that those who migrate through the Salvation Army are under a financial handicap of from $70 upwards.
That is just a plain statement of fact; it is not antagonistic, but it is the statement of the view taken by the department of the arrangement made between the Salvation Army and these boys. It is simply a matter of business; it may have been good policy or bad, but it was not done in any spirit of antagonism. We carried on negotiations with Commissioner Lamb without bitterness and I think I am giving the House all the information I have from memory.

Mr. Chairman, some time ago I asked the minister a question, and I think he has been given .sufficient time in which to consider it. My question was what other organizations and societies have had similar grants cut off, and the amounts of those grants.	.
The British Immigration and Colonization Association, of Montreal, and the Scottish Immigrant Aid Society. They have been getting these grants but they will be cut off this year.
Is that Father MacDon-nell's society?
Yes.
What society was that?
That is the Scottish Immigrant Aid Society, which brought out some Hebrideans and others.

A short time ago the minister said that all societies similar to the Salvation Army, which have been doing similar work in Canada with similar grants, had been cut off. I asked him for a list of those different societies and organizations and the amount in each case.

There were the two societies, the British Immigration and Colonization Association and the association of Father MacDonnell, the Scottish Immigrant Aid Society. These two societies have been getting grants until this year, but they will be cut off, and there are no other societies getting grants.
Are these not commercial organizations?
No.
What was the amount?

Rev. Dr. Smythe is the
head of the one organization and Father MacDonnell is the head of the other. They are both doing purely immigration work.
What salary does Rev. Dr. Smythe get?
My deputy informs me that he does not get anything from the department.
What salary does the other reverend gentleman get?
I do not know exactly.
Shall I tell the hon. gentleman? He gets $1,800.
I do not feel satisfied that I have an answer to my question yet. I asked for the amount in each case.
The one society received a grant of $5,000, while the other was paid $5,000 a year for the past four years.

Since the discussion on this item has broadened out into a consideration of some of the policies connected with immigration, there are a few points to which I should like to draw the attention of the minister and the House. The hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken) expressed himself a few moments ago as very strongly of the opinion that the department should reverse its policy with regard to child immigration. May I point out that the Canadian Council on Child Welfare has issued a memorandum in which it states:
Might we point out that Canadian child welfare opinion is as unanimous in opposing unaccompanied immigration to Canada of juveniles under fourteen years of age, as it is in opposing the continuous or the permanent employment of children, below this age, in any of the production enterprises of the Dominion.
And after quoting the Bondfield report the
memorandum says:
The Canadian Association of Child Protection Officers, comprising the governmental offi-
Supply-Immigra lion

eials engaged in child welfare work throughout the Dominion, the Council for Social Service of the Church of England in Canada, the National Council of Women in Canada, the Imperial Order of Daughters of the Empire, the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, the Social Service Council of Canada and the Canadian Council on Child Welfare, have all devoted special attention to the subject of juvenile immigration in the last five years and have issued special findings thereon. We would draw your ateention to the fact that they will be found in agreement in their attitude to this present regulation.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the department, is to be-highly commended for the stand that it has taken in this matter.
Further, with regard to the Salvation Army I take it that it is not a question as to whether or not the Salvation Army may be doing good religious work. It is a question as to whether or not the government should continue to give special privileges to one particular religious organization. The Army has been receiving certain special privileges, and I would say, as one who has been fairly closely identified with immigration work for the past twenty years, that although some very fine people have undoubtedly come out under the auspices of the Salvation Army, on the other hand there are very large numbers who have been quite unfitted for positions in this country and some of these have become a perpetual load upon Canada. It seems to me, therefore, that the department is to be condemned not so much for the action it has now taken, but rather for not earlier having taken action along this line. The sooner we come to the position indicated by the hon. member for Maoleod (Mr. Coote), cut off the grants to these various religious and private organizations and devote whatever money we are spending in that way to our own immigration service the better it will be for all concerned. Otherwise we are apt to have friction as between one and the other of these various private agencies. Anyone who has read the correspondence and the memoranda exchanged between the Salvation Army and the department will, I am inclined to think, be on the side of the department in this matter.
Again I should like to emphasize, that the department still seems to be content with bringing immigrants to this country without going into the question of thoroughly rooting them in Canada. I know the officials claim to place them, but the immigrants do not stay placed, partly because many of them are quite unfitted for the positions to which they come. In my own city of Winnipeg we have had within the last few months a very strong protest from the Social Welfare Commission of the city in which they indicate the very large

numbers of recent immigrants that are being supported by the city. I have under my hand scores of protests of this character which would take me an hour to read. They are from almost every labour organization in the country, because these quickly feel the effect of immigrants in an already congested labour market. I have also protests from a large number of other organizations. I think perhaps I might give this, from the Edmonton Board of Public Welfare, as very typical of a large number that have come to hand:
We find that the immigrants come to the west with the idea of farming, and all those brought out and assisted in passage come on this understanding. The fact that these men have drifted into town and are asking assistance from this municipality is prima facie evidence of their failure on the land. We have been unable to place these men in almost every instance in anything but temporary unskilled labouring jobs.
It would seem to me that the existence of a large number of oases of this kind is the best evidence we have that the policy of the Immigration department has not gone far enough, and I take it that whatever may be said with regard to the welfare of the immigrants, we in Canada must stand for the preservation of our own standards of living. There is not the slightest doubt that the dumping of a large number of immigrants into this country has very much accentuated the problem of unemployment in Canada.
Now the next point-and I am going to be just as brief as I can in bringing these matters to the attention of the department-is the prevalence of misrepresentation on the part of immigration agents on the other side of the water. Again and again I have asked questions of the minister with regard to these matters, and have received rather evasive replies. Here is a typical advertisement, from an old country paper:
14,000	Single Men Wanted For Farm Work in Canada
With and without experience. Assured employment and good wages.
Also families, domestics and boys.
Apply,
Chas. R. Compston and Son,
65, Church Street, Lancaster.
The advertisement goes on to state that a Canadian Pacific representative will be in attendance to select suitable applicants at reduced rates. Now, Mr. Chairman, I submit that it is not fair to the intending immigrant to suggest that if he comes to this country without experience he is going to get anything like steady work on the farm. Even the man with experience is not going to get work the

Supply-Immigration
year round on the farm, the inexperienced man is certain not to get it. The result is that thousands of these men come into our large distributing centres in the west just as soon as the harvest is over. The good wages offered do not convey any idea as to the real conditions here in Canada. The minister when I asked him a question along this line a few weeks ago said, "Oh, we cannot become responsible for all that the agents might say over in England." I urge that the minister in this country ought to be responsible. I am glad to say that as the result of questions asked on the floor of this House the authorities in the British parliament undertook to discipline some of the agents in England, and that can be readily done if the department here is alert. These advertisements inserted in the old country papers undoubtedly are misleading, and a great many people are induced to come to this country who, before they have been here very long, find themselves out of work and soon become dependent upon charity.
As to the character of the men who come to Canada, here, for example, is one out of a score of clippings I have from old country papers. I note that some hon. gentlemen seek to interrupt me. I think, Mr. Chairman, I gave place three or four times to some of these gentlemen in the comer to my right. Surely it is not necessary that desks should be banged during my remarks at this time. If the gentlemen cannot give any better reply than the banging of desks they could do that much more suitably outside rather than in a chamber that is supposed to devote itself to deliberative work. As to the character of the men employed I should like to refer to one or two statements given in the old country papers as affording some idea of how this problem of immigration is regarded in the old country. Here is one paragraph:
Forty-five young men, all of whom have been on the "dole", left London to-day in charge of the Canadian National railways en route for Canada, the first-fruits of the Ministry of Labour's farm training scheme, by which it is hoped to transform groups of unemployed single men into successful settlers overseas.
And again:	,
The men of this party all come from cities and towns, and are without previous agricultural experience. Before being accepted for this scheme they were carefully selected by the Ministry of Labour, and were approved by the Canadian Department of Immigration both before and after training. Some who on going to Claydon were under weight from lack of nourishment, have gained nearly a stone of solid flesh.
I have every sympathy with those who have been on the dole and others in the old country who are so reduced that a few weeks of help in a training colony will put them into better condition; but I would urge that men who are picked up on the streets of the big cities in the old country are not likely to make the most successful farmers out on our western prairies.

Maybe they would be all
right in New Brunswick.

It is suggested that
they might be all right in New Brunswick.
I sometimes wish that the government would dump into the eastern provinces as many people and of the same class as they have dumped into the west. It would not be long before we had some decidied protest from the east with regard to the immigration policy of the government. It is all very well for men in England to think of immigration as a means of getting rid of those whom they do not know what to do with there. Let me read a paragraph from the speech of Mr. Amery as given in the House of Commons as far back as the 27th July, 1925. Discussing the immigration problem he said:
I am tempted to read a few homely sentences from one west countryman's letter:
"I have quite a good farm. I have a real good cow and a calf, 18 chickens and one cock."
All these supplied to them.
"I bought one pig which is due to have little ones next month.
I see the papers in England say one cannot get worlf in Canada. I have five farmers after me to work for them. In any case I am downright pleased with my place and can make money out of it".
That is given as an example of a successfully placed farmer. He may make good; but I would suggest to any one who knows the prairie farms of the west, that one cow, a calf, eighteen chickens, a cock, and a brood sow, are not quite enough to start in on with any hopes of making a success. We ought to be practical in this matter. I can understand that kind of thing might appeal to people who are accustomed to allotment gardens in England and who have other ways of supplementing what they make out of those gardens, but we must recognize the actualities of life in the west.
Moreover I would point out that a very large number who are coming to this country not only were mechanics in the old country, but are rapidly finding themselves pushed into the industrial field in this country. Only a few days ago I had a letter from the mining district in the Crowsnest pass stating that already the newly arrived immigrants of this year were crowding into the mining areas where already there existed very serious un-
Supply-Immigration

employment. About a year ago I noticed in a paper called Canada published in Great Britain a report of certain speeches made by one Lieutenant-Colonel Robins. Among other things he said:
Ontario's industries, as well as its agriculture grow steadily, and we can find room for good artisans or mechanics as well as for trained farm hands who have been forced by home conditions to become dole drawers.
The purpose evidently is to bring out not merely farmers but mechanics, whether or not there is room for them in this country. Let me urge that notwithstanding what many boards of trade and railways may state, the immigration of large numbers of people to Canada is not the economic solution of our problems. It is frequently said that if we only have more people, we shall have more consumers in this country. Simply by multiplying the population of Canada by two or three, without altering the fundamental factors existing at any given time, does not offer any real solution of our economic difficulties. It is quite true that the railroads may be able to profit by the fares of these people; it is quite true that if the immigrants have capital, certain real estate or land colonization firms may profit, but that is not a real solution so far as the people at large are concerned. If we are to have immigrants, I would urge that we remember that we ought to be willing to assume the social responsibilities which their coming involves.' We in the west have had a heavy load to carry in endeavouring to assimilate the newly arrived immigrants. We have again and again petitioned, for example, that we should have help with regard to the upkeep of unemployed immigrants. We have also urged that we should have help with regard to sick immigrants. I have under my hand a letter from the superintendent of the hospital at Winnipeg, but I will not read it, because some hon. members may think it is only western propaganda. I will read instead an editorial from the Montreal Gazette in the hope that it may appeal to some of the eastern men more than protests which we might bring from the west. In an editorial under date of February 6, 1926, this statement is made with regard to immigrants and hospitals:
If the city is not responsible for the care extended to its immigrant population by the hospitals, then the obligation falls back upon the department of the government which brings these people to this country. . . . The immigrant, until he is able to take care of himself, or can assert some right of citizenship, is morally, at least a ward of the department which brings him into the country; certainly 
that department has no right to disclaim responsibility and remain inactive when the immigrant, in sickness and penury applies to Montreal hospitals for treatment,
That is the way some in Montreal feel about the question. We in the west have felt that way for a long time. I would simply repeat, without elaborating this point at all, that if we are going to bring in immigrants and believe they are an economic asset to this country, the least we can do is to assume the social responsibilities which their coming involves.
I want to emphasize that contention particularly with regard to the foreign-bom immigrant. I am informed by some of the outstanding officials connected with immigration that we cannot hope for any large numbers of farm immigrants from Great Britain. I am further informed that we have already largely exhausted the sources of supply in northern Europe, and that in the future we must more and more look to southeastern Europe for our immigrants. I have no particular quarrel with immigrants from southeastern Europe. Many of them are going to make good Canadian citizens; but it will take a generation before they can be thoroughly absorbed into our Canadian life, and it is cruel to bring them here and then denounce them because their religion, social life and political ideals are different from those of the Canadian people. Let us remember that if we insist on bringing in European immigrants, especially immigrants from southeastern Europe, we must be fully prepared to accommodate ourselves to the different social customs, religious practices and political aspirations which they bring with them.
There is only one further point that I venture to urge upon the government, and that is the more careful selection by the government of those who come to this country. If I understand aright, an agreement has been made with the railways by which, to all intents and purposes, the selection of immigrants is left in the hands of the railway authorities. I hope that when I sit down the minister will clear up this question. If I am correctly informed, within the last year or two an arrangement has been made with the railroads by which they undertake, almost entirely, to make the selection of the immigrants whom they think fit and have guaranteed1 that these immigrants will be safe!}' placed in this country. In my opinion that is an authority that ought not to be given up by the Dominion government. The Dominion government ieself ought to examine every immigrant and ought to be held responsible

Supply-Immigration
for the eare of every immigrant brought to this country. I would say that the Dominion government cannot hope effectively to avoid the responsibility for the placing of the immigrant in Canada. It is all very well to say that the Canadian Pacific Railway has made a careful selection and has guaranteed employment. What does that mean? It very often means that the railway company has secured the fare of the immigrant to this country, and afterwards, if they have found him a position, it has been done by ousting somebody else from that position. Thus the problem of unemployment is no nearer a solution than before; it is indeed increased. I ask the Minister of Immigration to give us in some detail the arrangement that exists between the department and the railways, both with regard to the selection and the placing of the immigrant.
The hon. member states that he wants an answer to that question. Which one? The last one?

My last question. I began with some general observations, but I closed by asking the minister to give me in some detail the arrangement that exists between the department and the railways both with regard to the selection of the immigrants on the other side of the water and the placing of them in Canada.

There is an agreement between the department and the two big railway corporations-there is no use in trying to say anything different-but I think we have the agreement in such shape that the department will control the inflow of immigrants and their character. I may say that they are doing a certain amount of recruiting in some of the countries in Europe. We have made an agreement with them that none of their recruiting agents will have any connection with the shipping agents, that no commissions will be paid to any of those men who are .doing the recruiting, that they will be paid a stated adequate salary, that they will have no inducement whatever to get immigrants so far as remuneration is concerned; and they undertake to bring no immigrants in Canada who are not of the agricultural class. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre found fault because some of those immigrants did not stay on t'he farm after they were placed there. I think it would be pretty difficult to make any man stay on the farm if he did not want to. The most we could ask from any association would be that they place those people on the farms to begin with.
I am going to make a statement with reference to the lack of employment, because I think I know about as much in regard to this question as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I have never seen a spring or summer in Manitoba, my own province, where we had a surplus of agricultural labour- always a shortage. There will be a shortage next month. The farmer members of this House realize that fact. Instead of a surplus of agricultural labour there will be a shortage. Then in regard to other classes of labour, an immense amount of work is going to be earned on in Canada during next summer. Some of us are optimistic-we are not all pessimists- and I think within six weeks from the present we will see the whole question of unemployment in Canada solved.
For how long?

I am no prophet and I cannot tell that. I know that when we had in Canada one-half the population that we have to-day there was a much larger percentage of unemployment than there is at present, and I claim that if we had twice the population the percentage of unemployment would be still less. Therefore an increase in population does not necesarily mean unemployment. I sympathize with the views of the Labour people, but they are afraid that if a labourer comes into this country he will put out of employment some other labourer in Canada. It does not work out that way. I have had some experience in regard to employment outside of farming. If we get the right class of people in Canada, people who are physically fit and are not afraid to work, the whole question of unemployment will solve itself. There will be some trouble next winter. Did hon. members ever see a winter which was entirely free from it? It is a concomitant of winter conditions in this country. We will have a certain amount of flotsam and jetsam; there is pathos and tragedy, and also humour, in this matter of immigration. I know that some things happen that are deplorable, but they will happen in connection with any immigration policy you like to adopt. There will be always a certain number of misfits, but is that any reason why we should not want people in our great wide open country, which indeed is waiting for people to take advantage of the opportunities offered to them when they come here? I would not have accepted the position of Minister of Immigration had I not great faith in the country and did I not believe that we could prosper with a much larger population

than we have. We need a greater population. I am attempting, with the little ability that I have, to carry on a policy of colonization that will, as far as is humanly possible, fit the immigrants into the places available for them. I cannot satisfy the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He takes a different point of view, looks at it from a different angle. But I believe I have as sane a view of the whole situation as my hon. friend has, looking at it from his angle. I do not say this with any bitterness, because I believe the hon. member is sincere. He lives in Winnipeg, and what he sees of the drift of some of the immigration gives him a view of the matter which perhaps he would not have did he live where I live and did he see conditions as I have seen them.

I do not intend at this time to attack or criticize the minister or the administration of his department. As a matter of fact I have found that there were some difficulties involved owing to the regulations. However, in the few cases that have come under my notice, if the department were approached and the matter argued out one would be apt to see the situation from the point of view of the department, and at the same time take what comfort one could out of a sane administration of the regulations. But it is against the regulations that I have a serious grievance. I know that some people who would make the very best immigrants are kept out of this country. I want the regulations changed. I want, as the minister says, a business administration of the immigration policy of Canada. One case I have in mind was that of three brothers and one sister who had established themselves :in Canada and were prosperous. They wanted to bring out their brother. He was earning his own living and was quite competent to do so in Canada, but owing to the fact that he had a maimed arm, and someone did not wish him to enter the Dominion, obstacle after obstacle was placed in his way. He is here now, is a respectable citizen, and will never become a charge upon the countiy. But the difficulty arises that when the immigrant starts on his journey to this country he must be routed through to destination. I wonder how many of us in early life would like to have been "routed through" in some country where we wanted to establish ourselves. I do not want to labour the point, but will read what is a sad commentary upon our immigration regulations. It is a letter written by a maidservant to a former employer, the head of a very large manufacturing concern well-

known throughout Canada. Under date of February 24, 1927, the girl writes:
Dear Mr. Blank,
Do you remember Lily, who stayed with you last year for a few weeks while Eunice was having her holidays? May I ask you a favour?
I intend to bring my brother out here this spring. It would be easy for him to get the immigration permission, as he is of Swiss nationality, skilled, in good health, and would bring about $1,000 with him-but the Canadian condition is, that he has a position in view or at least that he can prove he has relations which would help him to find work.
Knowing nobody else who could do anything for him in that respect I bring the matter up to you and would be very grateful for your kind advice.
My brother is twenty-one years of age-a competent electrician, radio man, mechanic and car driver. We had a little factory (with about fifty labourers) of that kind in Basle, Switzerland, and my father was very keen that my brother should learn everything, practically and theoretically, concerning "appareillages electriques".
The great service you could do for him would be to let me have just a few lines, saying that you are interested in my brother and you would assist him to find work when he comes to Canada.
I realize that I ask much-perhaps too much -but I stress the fact that it would be merely "pro forma" and that you would not be under any obligation whatever. You would help a young man who certainly deserves it, who is earnest, industrious and does not come with erroneous illusions, but who has the firm will to set to work and to do any work if necessary. As a further asset he has a fairly good knowledge of the English language.
Thanking you in advance in my brother's and my own name for your great kindness I remain,
Respectfully yours,
Lillie Ritter.
Imagine a man with those qualifications not being allowed to enter Canada! Or if he does come in with $1,000 in his pocket, the idea is abroad that he must be projected towards some definite spot to do some definite thing, although we are crying for immigrants. When the regulations are such that a personal entreaty of this kind is thought necessary to a man who is not in any sense interested other than from having been for a short time the employer of the girl who writes the letter, I say it is time that they were changed. Therefore I ask the minister to assure the committee that a man well educated, with money in his pocket, anxious to grow up with this country and become a good citizen, shall not be denied entrance because he cannot say: I am definitely going to be employed by A. B., and I am going to do thus and so. I know a man who, having said that he had a job as a shoemaker in a

Has he any supervision of the publicity work which is carried on by other agents and which has been referred to as misrepresentation of conditions in Canada?
Those agents are really the agents of some of the steamship companies. They may paint matters a little too rosily, but I do not know what we can do to supervise such advertising.

The director of
publicity might oversee the advertisements and the publicity matter before it is put out as representative of Canada.

We have asked for cooperation between some of the steamship companies and the department. Some cooperate and some do not. I went over to Great Britain some twenty years ago on immigration work, and at that time I found that the Department of Immigration was employing steamship agents as Canadian agents in the old country. I found a great deal of fault with that. I found issued by steamship agents in regard to Canada pamphlets and other literature which was altogether too rosy and something which I did not like at all. Advertisements of that character are still being issued to some extent by steamship agents, not by us.

The department
must assume the responsibility. There could not be any objection to the department making this publicity agent an overseer of the publicity campaign carried on in the old country.

Some shipping companies
under British registry who want to get immigrants to come to Canada in order to benefit by their fares may make statements that are not altogether true, statements that are a little too rosy and that perhaps convey a false impression, but I do not know what the department can do in regard to suppressing them. If those companies were willing to accept advertisements prepared by the department, the matter would be different.

What are the
functions and duties of the immigration investigating officer?

If I have to answer all questions in regard to every officer of the department I am up against a difficult task. I think we have just one thousand employees in the Immigration department, in Canada, overseas, and in the United States. My deputy informs me that this investigation officer is largely engaged in taking care of the boundary line between United States and Canada, investigating complaints regarding people passing backwards and forwards.

I intend to go into the
immigration policy of the government at a later date, on item 56, which I believe will be the proper item. I may say now that I am very glad indeed that the government have centralized their immigration agencies between the department and the two railways. Are the agencies overlapping in any way on the continent, in England or in the United States, or are they using in any of those places the same agencies or the same officers? It does not matter which of these agencies spends money in bringing out immigrants, because if we do not pay it in taxation we pay it in freight rates.

No, there is no overlapping in that regard, because we have practically no other immigration agents on the continent of Europe than the government immigration agent at the point of embarkation. Of course there is a different arrangement in Great Britain.

The minister referred to
the immigration agent that the Alberta government has in London. That province has suffered in years past through having immigrants dumped on them, and I believe the official in London is placed there by the Alberta government more to direct colonization than to obtain immigrants.

During the early part
of the debate to-night some reference was made to a system of permits. Can the minister tell us how many were issued last year, how many the year before, and under whose authority they were issued?
Some time ago I laid on the table of the House a statement showing the number of permits that were issued.

That will be all right.

I did not intend to read
any oi these letters to-night, but I will have to read another letter now. This letter says:
I signed a document agreeing to pay to the Salvation Army the sum of $100 with the understanding that it was for my transportation to Canada and not as a contribution to Army funds. This document is in England. I think other boys are repaying the money with the same idea. Those who enter farther into Canada have more than $100 to pay, therefore, it must appear to be the cost of passage. I was on a training farm for three months, but this was termed to be free.
I have several of those letters.
What is the date?
I have not got it.

What would be the
cost of transportation?
We make a grant of $80 for the passage money, but I do not think it costs that much.

This country pays so much passage money for the boys and the Imperial government pays so much. What is the actual cost of the passage? We would like to know whether the Salvation Army is asking for more than the cost of transportation.

It is $55. I think all societies engaged in immigration work are getting the same grant. They receive more than it really costs them, and they have a surplus in case of immigrants going to places east of Winnipeg. If an immigrant goes to Winnipeg it will take about the amount of the grant.
They have to eat on the way.
In the case of boys going west of Winnipeg, the combined grant of the Imperial and Dominion governments is $100.

If you are making a grant of a certain stum you surely know what it costs to bring them over. If you do not know what it costs you are not in a position to say whether the Salvation Army is charging for the passage or for the outfit of the boys.
What does it cost to bring a boy to Toronto or Winnipeg?
They get a reduced rate.

If the minister has not the figure before him he can furnish it later. If we know the actual cost of bringing the boys over then we will be*in a position to separate the transportation cost from the outfit cost and we will know exactly what the Salvation Army has been doing with these boys.
All right.
